titre: Analysis for event tracking order in cosmos DB
description:
Analysis: Why Use Redis SDK Instead of Cosmos DB for Event Tracking

1️⃣ Performance Considerations

  • Redis: Ultra-fast in-memory storage, capable of handling millions of operations per second with microsecond latency.
  • Cosmos DB: Even with point reads, latency is higher due to network and disk-based storage (~10ms+ per operation).
  • Conclusion: Redis SDK provides real-time event tracking with significantly lower latency.

2️⃣ Scalability & High Throughput

  • Redis: Scales horizontally with clustering, handling massive concurrent requests efficiently.
  • Cosmos DB: Uses Request Units (RU/s) which limit the number of operations per second. Scaling requires higher costs.
  • Conclusion: Redis is more efficient for high-frequency event tracking.

3️⃣ Cost Efficiency

  • Redis: No RU-based pricing; cost depends on memory usage.
  • Cosmos DB: More operations = higher RU consumption, making frequent event writes costly.
  • Conclusion: Redis provides a cost-effective solution for real-time event tracking.

4️⃣ Real-Time Event Processing & Deduplication

  • Redis: Supports Pub/Sub, Streams, and Sorted Sets for real-time event tracking & deduplication.
  • Cosmos DB: Requires Change Feed processing, which is slower for real-time deduplication.
  • Conclusion: Redis is designed for fast event processing and deduplication.

5️⃣ Existing Microservice Consistency

  • Other microservices already use Redis SDK → Standardizing across microservices simplifies maintenance.
  • Cosmos DB would introduce inconsistent event handling approaches across services.
  • Conclusion: Sticking to Redis SDK maintains a unified event processing strategy.

Final Decision: Redis SDK for Event Tracking

✅ Ultra-low latency for real-time event tracking.
✅ Higher scalability & throughput without RU limitations.
✅ Lower cost for frequent operations.
✅ Supports real-time deduplication & event processing efficiently.
✅ Consistent with existing microservices using Redis SDK.

Implementation Plan

  1. Use Redis for real-time event tracking & deduplication.
  2. Use Redis TTL to auto-clean old events & reduce memory usage.

description:
Overview

  • As user, I want to have an updated view on the ticket which are currently listed for the resource. Then when you new downtime ticket are detected on machine, the system automatically update the table displaying this new ticket in it. No need to reinstance/refresh the list from operators.

      Technology porpostition: WebSockets via Socket.IO

  • WebSockets provide a persistent, bidirectional connection between the frontend and backend.
  • Socket.IO is selected for its ease of implementation, automatic reconnection handling, and broader browser support.
  • The backend will emit an event upon new ticket creation, which the frontend will listen to and update the UI dynamically.

2. Solution Flow

    2.1. Initial Connection

       1️⃣ The frontend establishes a WebSocket connection with the backend upon page load.
       2️⃣ The backend acknowledges the connection and assigns a unique identifier (e.g., session ID) to the client.

   2.2. Ticket Ingestion & Event Emission

      3️⃣ When a new downtime ticket is inserted during ingestion, the backend detects this change.
      4️⃣ The backend emits a newDowntimeTicket event via WebSockets to notify all connected clients (downtime-ui for in our case).


3. WebSocket Architecture

    3.1. Backend Responsibilities

  • Maintain a WebSocket server to manage client connections.
  • Listen for new ticket insertions in the database.
  • Emit a newDowntimeTicket event to all connected clients when a new ticket is created.

    3.2. Frontend Responsibilities

  • Establish a WebSocket connection to the backend.
  • Listen for the newDowntimeTicket event and dynamically update the downtime table.

   2.3. Frontend UI Update

     5️⃣ The frontend receives the newDowntimeTicket event and updates the displayed list dynamically.
     6️⃣ Operators see the new ticket instantly, without refreshing the page.


Why is this the "right/best" solution?

✅ Instant Updates → The backend emits an event (newDowntimeTicket) immediately when a new ticket is inserted, ensuring the frontend updates in real time.
✅ No Manual Refresh → Operators don’t need to refresh the page, as updates are pushed automatically.
✅ Efficient Communication → Instead of polling the backend continuously, WebSockets establish a persistent connection, reducing unnecessary API calls.
✅ Scalability Consideration → If multiple users are viewing the same resource, they all receive updates simultaneously, improving user experience.

Azure SQL Database Restore
description:
Pipeline or portal guidelines on how to restore an Azure SQL Database.

Initial Guidance

To perform a point-in-time restore of an Azure SQL Database using Terraform, you can follow these general steps:

  1. Create a New Database for Restore: Use the Azure portal, PowerShell, or the REST API to create a new database from a point-in-time backup. Unfortunately, this step cannot be directly managed by Terraform[1].
  2. Import the New Database into Terraform State: After creating the new database, you need to import it into your Terraform state. This ensures that Terraform is aware of the new resource and can manage it going forward.

Plain Text
   terraform import azurerm_sql_database.example /subscriptions/{subscriptionId}/resourceGroups/{resourceGroupName}/providers/Microsoft.Sql/servers/{serverName}/databases/{databaseName}


  1. Update Terraform Configuration: Modify your Terraform configuration to include the new database. This might involve updating variables, resource names, and other configurations to reflect the restored database.
  2. Apply Changes: Run terraform apply to apply the changes and ensure that your Terraform state is in sync with the actual resources.

Here is a simplified example of how your Terraform configuration might look:

Plain Text
provider "azurerm" {
  features {}
}

resource "azurerm_sql_server" "example" {
  name                         = "example-sqlserver"
  resource_group_name          = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  location                     = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  version                      = "12.0"
  administrator_login          = "adminuser"
  administrator_login_password = "H@Sh1CoR3!"
}

resource "azurerm_sql_database" "example" {
  name                = "example-sqldatabase"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  server_name         = azurerm_sql_server.example.name
  edition             = "Standard"
  requested_service_objective_name = "S1"
}


  1. Update Application Configuration: Ensure that your application configuration is updated to point to the new database instance.

These steps should help you manage a point-in-time restore of an Azure SQL Database using Terraform. If you need more detailed guidance, you can refer to the official Azure documentation[1].

If you have any specific questions or run into issues, feel free to ask!

Container App Authentication configuration With PingFederate and Easy Auth
description:
Target

Support ping federate as an identity provider in the container app external ingress auth config

Simultaneous Support for entra id and ping federate

  • In the container app environment auth config (infra level), add ping federate as an additional identity provider. Which means we support both.
  • When a UI uses ping federate then:
    • Entra Id will be disabled for the UI
    • The UI App acquires token from ping federate and goes through the ping federate backend config (app level)

Several Identity Providers in Container App

According to initial homework and prototyping, enabling two identity providers simultaneously in the container app env requires disabling the authorization check at the container app level meaning that it needs to be enforced at the app level.

In this scenario, container app auth config, only acts as a token validator against the configured identity provider injecting claims in downstream requests to be taken in consideration by the app.

=> Conclusion: requires development effort

Ping Federate as an Identity provider for Container app auth config

After configuration done by SSO team yesterday(new backend client_id), we have been able to successfully:

  • Acquire ID Tokens from ping federate with postman via Authorization code Flow with PKCE
  • Use Ping Federate as the single Identity provider in the container app env:
    • Was tested successfully by authenticating backend requests with bearer token coming from Ping Federate

Proposed Solution: since now we have all ui projects aligned with using ping federate, once all uis deployed, we can start switching the identity provider in dev and start our tests.

Separate Ping Federate Client Ids for front end and backend

As per SSO team confirmation, we can have two client ids one for front end and one for backend:
  • mes_xo: front end client id with Authorization Code PKCE Grant Type without client secret
  • mes_xo_backend: backend client id with Client Credentials Grant Type with client secret
Unfortunately, even if it is possible to introspect tokens generated with mes_xo from mes_xo_backend, when configured in container app mes_xo_backend does not authorize tokens from mes_xo.

In addition:
  • not possible to configure audience claims on the tokens
  • not possible to have 1 client id supporting all grant types without required usage of client secret (in the frontend)
This leaves us with 3 options:
  1. Rely fully on Azure Container App Authentication
    1. Impact: Remove Ping federate authentication behavior from uis and rely on tokens being present
    2. Pros: Least workload as everything is delegated to container app auth config
    3. Cons: Solution coupled to Azure Container App
  2. Introduce an open authorization endpoint
    1. Impact: Development of a backend endpoint that accepts a front end id token, validates it and provides a backend token
    2. Pros: Less coupled to container app
    3. Cons: Changes on all uis and 1 backend
  3. Rely fully on custom implementation (backed by library)
    1. Impact: Workloads in all uis and backend
    2. Pros: fully independent of container app
    3. Cons: consequent workload

Conclusion

After implementing easy auth in all environments with the mes_xo_backend app registration from ping federate:
  • We are able to use 7accounts in prod
  • UI based authentication becomes obsolete and has been removed
  • Easy auth cookie lifetime is configurable and settable to multiple days
However:
  • Not possible to refresh cookie before expiration to prevent session expiration
  • No rolling expiration available for cookies
oauth2-proxy offers a more flexible cookie capabilities and will be implemented as part of #121994

titre: Analyses issue related to refresh list of plants on subscribe topic plants in ingestion microservice
description:
While testing the snapshot to validate the filter for new plants in production, I noticed that the list was not updated with the new data from the Get Plant API.

First, I checked whether the ingestion of Pub/Sub in the container was correct, then verified that the event was published correctly from the PLT HRY API. After that, I rechecked the log stream by triggering the same pipeline, as we couldn't check the logs directly due to the max log limit.

I observed that the subscription was happening, but the list remained unchanged, indicating a synchronization issue. Additionally, there was a strange issue where I kept receiving the same list even after triggering the pipeline a second time.

While testing locally, I confirmed the synchronization issue and fixed it by adding two await statements in the fetchPlant and getPlant functions. However, the issue related to the Redis state not updating did not appear in the local environment.

For now, the issue has been addressed, but we are continuing to monitor whether the Redis save problem persists as we don't have access to Redis insight in prod env.

titre: technical analyse for creating  api that retrieves changes related to the downtime causes
description:
1. API Overview

We will develop an API that  retrieves changes related to the downtime causes.

2. API Inputs

  • plant (Mandatory)
  • lastTimeStamp (Optional) → Used for incremental updates; when absent, full data initialization occurs.

3. API Behavior

  • Retrieves changes related to downtime causes once per week.

4. Levels Determination Logic

  • Level 1: If parent_cause = NULL, it is a Level 1 cause.
  • Level 2: If parent_cause is between 1 and 5, it is a Level 2 cause.
  • Level 3: If parent_cause > 5 or any other value, it is a Level 3 cause.

5. Status Retrieval Logic

  • Level 2 Deactivation: If a Level 2 cause is deactivated, its status and all associated Level 3 sub-causes will be marked as inactive.
  • Level 3 Deactivation: If a Level 3 cause is deactivated, the entire status will be inactive.

6. API Output Structure

The API response will return data in the following format:

 

{

  "level1_id": "",

  "level1_description": "",

  "level2_id": "",

  "level2_description": "",

  "level3_id": "",

  "level3_description": "",

  "family": "",

  "plc_id": [array of resources],

  "status": "active/inactive"

}

 

 

7. Additional APIs

API for Retrieving Family

  • Retrieves the family for a downtime cause from the cause_family_assign table in the repos production-api .

API for Retrieving plc_id (Array of Resources)

  • Level 1 Causes: Retrieves all resources for the specified plant (handled in downtime backend).
  • Level 2 Causes:
    • Uses the resource_family-assign table to check family assignments.
    • If assigned to a family → Retrieves resources from the same family.
    • If not assigned to a family → Retrieves all the resources from plant
  • Level 3 Causes:
    • Resources will mirror the resources assigned to its parent Level 2 cause.

titre: Materialized View Processor Cost Optimization via Horizontal Scaling
description:
Initial

To optimize materialized view processor cost while preserving reasonable performance, proposal is to configure container app replica with small resources with possibility to auto-scale based on pubsub topic queue length to manage peak loads. 

Note that we assume that:
  • single replica with high resources is too expensive
  • not possible to scale to 0 since scheduled orchestrator is always generating work
  • small replica with autoscale will be more cost effective while preserving reasonable performance

Update 1 (04-03-2025)

Materialized view processor is not horizontally scalable due to a replica in memory component containing data that can be lost during replica teardown. (mail discussion attached).

picking-mp-alert
description:
We encountered the same issue with picking-mp, where the 1-second default timeout was too aggressive under load. We should also update the health probe timeout to 5 seconds for mp and data ingestion to ensure stability. @Chedy MISSAOUI 

Alert Reference:
https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Monitoring_Alerts/AlertDetails.ReactView/alertId~/%2fsubscriptions%2fbed82672-330b-4915-9395-19ff3f706716%2fresourceGroups%2frg-gptmpxn01-dev-eun-mes-01%2fproviders%2fMicrosoft.AlertsManagement%2falerts%2f8aaf9f48-5889-43bb-a062-7448fb65f000/invokedFrom/CopyLinkFeature

Update 1

  • Materialized view processors have a high replica restart time overtime
  • The following is the replica restart count last 3 days from 05/03/205 12:46 UTC

Inspecting the logs in the period of interest of the referenced alert (03/05/2025 01:00 -> 9:00 utc) shows readiness and liveliness probes issues:


Since readiness probe timeout is configured to 5 seconds for picking mp, we assume that these failures are related to dapr side car probes.

Leading us to think that overload of the replica is causing readiness endpoints to not respond successfully within the time out

Suggestion: decrease the materialized view orchestrator tempo to 5 seconds in dev and 2 seconds in ppr 

Update 2 (06/03/2025)

In dev environment setting interval to 1500 ms seems to eliminate replica restarts:

The following is the last 24 hours picking-mp dev replica restarts at 06/03/2025 09:43 utc

As replica restart count is high in ppr also, trying to set it to 900 ms to observe the impact => changes done at 06/03/2025 10:20 utc, observing...

Update 3 (07/03/2025)

setting orchestrator delay to 900 ms seems to have effect on the replica restart count:

The following is the last 24 hours picking-mp ppr replica restarts at 07/03/2025 14:20 utc


However:
  • Replica restart increase back to 1 after a while + without signs of restart in the console and system logs (Strange)
We will align dev and ppr on a 900 ms delay observing...

Update 4 (10/03/2025)

Setting interval to 900ms has:
  • Positive impact on lvl-mp in dev and ppr
  • No impact on picking-mp in dev and ppr where it is exhibiting a strange and high restart trend still
The following is the last 3 days picking-mp ppr replica restarts at 10/03/2025 10:20 utc


Conclusion

  • picking-mp as a service seems to require a lot of resource and a high timeout/low frequency health probes
  • picking-mo scheduling interval will be set to 2000ms in dev
  • scheduling interval will be set to 900 ms for lvl-mo and picking-mo in dev and ppr

titre: Analysis : technical solution update the pub/sub + websocket mechanisme for auto refresh
description:
1. Initial State (Before the Update)

Architecture and Workflow:

  • The ingestion microservice publishes a message to a topic using a publish-subscribe (Pub/Sub) mechanism. The published message is a simple string representing an event or update.
  • The backend service subscribes to this topic to receive the message and emits it to connected clients through a WebSocket connection.
  • Clients receive the message as a raw string and must process it to understand its content.
  • To display the updated information, clients triggers the data fetching api, causing a complete reload of data.

Key Issue:

  • Performance Bottleneck: High network bandwidth and CPU usage due to repeated reloads/fetches, especially with frequent updates/inserts.

2. Proposed State (After the Update)

Architecture and Workflow:

  • The ingestion microservice publishes a structured data object (representing the ticket) directly to the Pub/Sub topic.
  • The backend service receives the structured data and directly emits it via WebSocket to connected clients.
  • Clients receive the structured ticket data and update their internal store without refreshing the page.
  • The UI is immediately updated with the new or modified ticket data, maintaining real-time responsiveness.

Benefits:

  • Improved Real-Time Experience: Updates are seamlessly reflected on the client side without any page refresh.
  • Efficient Data Handling: Sending structured data reduces the need for serialization and parsing, leading to lower latency.
  • Lower Resource Consumption: Eliminates unnecessary page reloads, reducing both client and server resource utilization.


After discussing the proposed solution in a meeting, we agreed to make the auto-refresh mechanism more targeted and efficient. Instead of emitting events globally for every update, we will emit events specifically by resource and plant. This means that only the concerned plant and resource will receive the auto-refresh WebSocket event, significantly reducing unnecessary traffic and processing on clients that are not impacted by the update.

This targeted approach not only improves performance but also ensures that real-time updates are only triggered for the relevant users, making the system more efficient and scalable. It also minimizes bandwidth usage and reduces the load on both the server and client sides, especially when dealing with frequent updates or inserts.

description:
The goal was to improve how downtime ticket data is handled in the system. Previously, a simple string was sent to the backend, but now the process has been updated to send structured downtime ticket data instead.

  1. Ingestion Update:

    • Instead of sending a plain string to then perform a full refresh, we now publish downtime ticket data to the backend.

    • This ensures that the backend receives a complete data rather than just a reference then making a fetch everytime

  2. Backend Processing:

    • The backend now properly receives and processes the downtime ticket object.

    • After processing, the backend emits the downtime ticket event back to the client.

  3. Frontend Update:

    • On receiving the emitted event from the backend, the client updates its store with the new downtime ticket data.

    • This ensures that the UI reflects the latest state of the downtime ticket in real-time.

titre: Manage generic topic at orchestrator side
description:
The proposed improvement is to keep the orchestrator as a scheduler only, as it currently includes logic for handling messages from each topic. The idea is to subscribe to topics that start with topic_ by using a wildcard subscription (topic.*). However, caution is needed to avoid unintended subscriptions to topics containing the prefix topic_ that should not be managed.

Instead of having multiple subscribers and separate message handlers for each topic, there will be a single subscriber and a single message handling function. This function will forward both the message and the topic to the processor. At the processor level, the topic received from the orchestrator will be checked, and the necessary processing will be performed accordingly.

We need to pay close attention because, for example, we have a topic called TOPIC_PLANTS, which includes the TOPIC_ prefix. However, its message handling differs from other topics. Therefore, when subscribing to topics that start with TOPIC_, we must account for this by either excluding TOPIC_PLANTS or finding an alternative way to manage it.

Horizontal scaling for multiple replicas - partition key check
description:
Hello Jacques and Ling Fung,

 

We’ve been analyzing the potential limitations that may arise when autoscaling our ingestion microservices, and here are our findings:

 

1. EventHub Topic Handling Challenges

The primary challenge we face with autoscaling is managing our EventHub topics. Most of our EventHub topics have a partition key set to plant, but we’ve identified a few exceptions that do not use partition keys:

  • CUST → customerDef: ship-di
  • OUTBD_DEL, OUTBD_DEL_DTL → outboundDelivery (no plant) depends on outboundDeliveryDtl: ship-di
  • MTL → material: master-di

This lack of partition keys may lead to two major issues:

 

Issue 1: Out-of-Order Processing

  • When receiving two events from the same topic, each event may be handled by different replicas of the ingestion container.
  • This could result in the update operation being processed before the create operation, leading to a "not found" error and outdated data.
  • Proposed Solution:
  • Implement upserts in all ingestion services to ensure data consistency. Since our master data is in MII, a "not found" error in MES indicates missing data. In such cases, we will insert the data to maintain consistency.

 

Issue 2: Concurrency Issues in LSN Handling

  • If two events from the same topic are processed by different ingestion replicas simultaneously, concurrency issues may occur when the Redis SDK checks the LSN (Log Sequence Number), potentially resulting in outdated data.

 

 

2. Cross-Topic Event Synchronization Challenges

Our system also relies on processing related events from different topics (e.g., pickingOrder and shopOrder). When these events are handled by separate replicas, it can introduce additional issues:

Issue 1: Impact on Cache Consistency:

  • If one container processes data faster than another due to uneven partition loads or synchronization delays, cached data may expire before corresponding data from other events arrives, leading to inconsistencies.

 

Proposed Solution:

  • Increase TTL (Time to Live) for cached events to minimize data loss due to replica synchronization issues.

 

Issue 2: Concurrency in Cache Handling:

We’ve previously encountered concurrency issues in cache handling within a single replica, where two processes tried to access the same key simultaneously and found it empty. This led to duplicate key creation and incomplete data insertion. We resolved this by implementing a MutexManager to lock cache operations by key on Dapr state.

 

Current Challenge with Multiple Replicas:

  • With autoscaling, the challenge now becomes managing cache concurrency across multiple replicas.

 

Additionally, this is a proposal from @MISSAOUI Chedy (external) to improve the system by consolidating dependent topics into a single one.

 

 

Please let us know your thoughts on these findings and proposed solutions, as well as any suggestions for addressing the remaining open points without solutions.

We’re happy to discuss further and refine our approach based on your input.

 

 

Best regards,

Neji Ghazouani

description:
Summary of the Trigger-Based Solution for Picking Order Updates

We implemented two SQL Server triggers to automatically update the picking_order table whenever changes occur in related tables:

  • trg_update_picking_order_rescheduler_wk_history: Updates picking_order when a record in rescheduler_wk_history is updated.

  • trg_update_picking_order_alert: Updates picking_order when a record in alert is updated.

Each trigger:
✅ Updates timestamps (updated_at, rescheduler_wk_history_updated_at, alert_updated_at) in picking_order automatically.
✅ Ensures consistency between picking_order and related tables without requiring additional queries in application code.

Why Triggers Are a Better Choice than TypeORM Listeners or Manual Updates

1️⃣ Compared to TypeORM Listeners

TypeORM offers event listeners/hooks (@AfterUpdate, @BeforeUpdate) that could track updates in rescheduler_wk_history and alert and manually update picking_order.

🔴 Drawbacks of TypeORM Listeners:

  • Application-Level Overhead: Runs in the application layer, increasing processing time.

  • Potential Data Inconsistency: If the app crashes mid-transaction, the update to picking_order might not happen.

  • Complex Dependency Management: Requires ensuring the right repository/service is injected for updates.

✅ Why Triggers Are Better:

  • Runs directly at the database level, ensuring updates happen instantly and atomically.

  • No need for extra database calls from the application.

  • Works even if the application goes down or restarts.

2️⃣ Compared to Manual Updates in Code

We could also update picking_order manually in the application code whenever rescheduler_wk_history or alert is updated.

🔴 Drawbacks of Manual Updates:

  • Extra Query Execution: Every update in rescheduler_wk_history or alert requires a separate update query for picking_order.

  • Risk of Missing Updates: If the developer forgets to add the update logic in all necessary places, picking_order can become outdated.

  • Concurrency Issues: If multiple updates happen at the same time, there’s a chance of race conditions leading to outdated data.

✅ Why Triggers Are Better:

  • Automatic and Reliable: Ensures updates happen consistently without needing extra logic in the app.

  • No Extra Queries: Reduces the number of queries executed by the application, improving efficiency.

[Analysis]: Design interface for database access
description:
Detailed Architecture for Database Abstraction with TypeORM

This approach ensures a scalable, maintainable, and flexible database abstraction layer by combining:

  1. Abstract service for database operations.

  2. Concrete implementations for SQL Server and PostgreSQL using TypeORM.

  3. Dynamic dependency injection based on environment variables (DATABASE_TYPE).

  4. Abstraction for TypeORM to maintain consistency in entity management.

  5. CI/CD deployment strategy for cloud (SQL Server) and edge (PostgreSQL) environments.

1. Overview of the Approach

We will create an abstract service (DatabaseService) defining the contract for database operations.

  • Two implementations:

    • SQLDatabaseService (for SQL Server)

    • PostgresDatabaseService (for PostgreSQL)

  • Dynamic selection using dependency injection and environment variables (DATABASE_TYPE).

  • TypeORM abstraction to keep repository access consistent and reusable.

  • Single repository, multiple deployments (Cloud → SQL Server, Edge → PostgreSQL).

2. Architectural Design & Implementation Strategy

2.1. Abstract Service Class (DatabaseService)

  • This abstract class will define the standard CRUD operations.

  • Implementations will extend this class and use TypeORM repositories.

2.2. TypeORM Repository Abstraction (BaseRepository)

  • A generic base repository will provide common database operations using TypeORM.

  • Concrete services (SQL/PostgreSQL) will extend this repository to ensure consistency.

2.3. Concrete Implementations (SQL & PostgreSQL Services)

Each database service will:

  • Extend DatabaseService and implement logic using TypeORM.

  • Use dependency injection to inject the correct repository.

  • Ensure scalability by following TypeORM best practices.

2.4. Dynamic Database Selection Using Dependency Injection

A database provider will:

  1. Check the DATABASE_TYPE environment variable.

  2. If PostgreSQL (DATABASE_TYPE=postgres), bind PostgresDatabaseService.

  3. Otherwise, default to SQL Server (SqlDatabaseService).

3. TypeORM Abstraction & Entity Management

3.1. Abstracting TypeORM Repository (BaseRepository)

  • A generic repository will be created using TypeORM’s Repository class.

  • This ensures code reusability across both database implementations.

4. Environment Configuration and Deployment Strategy

4.1. Environment Variable Handling (DATABASE_TYPE)

Environment Variable

Database Used

Deployment

DATABASE_TYPE=sql

SQL Server

Cloud

DATABASE_TYPE=postgres

PostgreSQL

Edge

Not Set

SQL Server (Default)

Cloud

4.2. Deployment with Different Images

  • Cloud Image → Uses SQL Server

  • Edge Image → Uses PostgreSQL 

  • CI/CD pipelines will generate separate images for each deployment.

5. Summary & Benefits

✔ Abstraction for both database logic (DatabaseService) and TypeORM (BaseRepository).
✔ Dynamic selection based on DATABASE_TYPE, ensuring flexibility.
✔ TypeORM repositories ensure consistency across database types.
✔ Single repository → Reduces code duplication.
✔ Separate cloud and edge deployments → Ensures scalability.

Please find below a simple example for the implementation: 
Commit c8fb2081: Decoupling via strategy pattern - Repos

Differences Between PostgreSQL and SQL Implementations

Feature

PostgreSQL (PostgresDatabaseService)

SQL (SqlDatabaseService)

Primary Key

@PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')

@PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment') (SQL Server)

Pagination Handling

Uses LIMIT & OFFSET

Uses TOP (SQL Server) 

JSON Handling

Has native JSONB type

SQL Server has limited JSON support

String Length Limit

Uses TEXT for long strings

 SQL Server needs NVARCHAR(MAX)

Boolean Type

Uses BOOLEAN

SQL Server uses BIT

Timestamp Handling

CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is standard

SQL Server may require DEFAULT GETDATE()

private async processOutboundMessageWithCache(
  plant: number,
  message: RedisMessage,
  redisStore: string,
): Promise<void> {
  const context = DaprService.createLogContext(
    'processOutboundMessageWithCache',
    plant,
  );

  const { mappedData, sourceTable, destination, operation } =
    message;

  const cacheKey = `${mappedData.outbound}.${operation}`;
  const operationInfo = {
    name: '',
    srcLocation: 'processOutboundMessageWithCache',
  };
  const operationDetails = { cacheKey, plant };

  // Acquire lock for this key
  this.customLogger.debug(`Locking key for ${cacheKey}`, context);
  operationInfo.name = 'Acquire lock for outbound';
  const release = await execAndLog(
    this.customLogger,
    context,
    () =>
      acquireLockWithTimeout(
        this.customLogger,
        context,
        this.mutexManagerService,
        cacheKey,
      ),
    operationInfo,
    operationDetails,
  );

  if (!release) {
    this.customLogger.error(
      `Failed to acquire lock for ${cacheKey}, skipping.`,
      context,
    );
    await moveToDeadLetterQueue(
      this.customLogger,
      context,
      redisStore,
      this.daprClient,
      cacheKey,
      message,
      MESSAGE_ACTION.GETORDERID,
    );
    return;
  }

  try {
    operationInfo.name = 'Get state';
    const cachedState = await execAndLog(
      this.customLogger,
      context,
      () => this.daprClient.state.get(redisStore, cacheKey),
      operationInfo,
      operationDetails,
    );

    const cacheValue = cachedState.valueOf();
    const recordCache = {
      destination,
      keysValue,
      mappedData,
      sourceTable,
    };

    if (!cacheValue || cacheValue.sourceTable === sourceTable) {
      // First entry or continuing same source
      await appendAndSaveToCache(
        this.customLogger,
        this.daprClient,
        redisStore,
        cacheKey,
        cacheValue,
        recordCache,
      );

      if (sourceTable === 'outboundeldtl') {
        // Emit if it's the detail record
        await emitSqlEvent(
          this.customLogger,
          context,
          this.eventEmitter,
          destination,
          mappedData,
          operation,
        );
      }
      return;
    }

    // If different sourceTable is already in cache
    const cachedMappedData = cacheValue.mappedData;
    const cachedDestination = cacheValue.destination;

    if (sourceTable === 'outboundel') {
      // Add plant to current data from cached
      mappedData.plant = cachedMappedData.plant;
      await emitSqlEvent(
        this.customLogger,
        context,
        this.eventEmitter,
        destination,
        mappedData,
        operation,
      );
    } else if (sourceTable === 'outboundeldtl') {
      // Add plant to cached data from current message
      cachedMappedData.plant = mappedData.plant;

      await emitSqlEvent(
        this.customLogger,
        context,
        this.eventEmitter,
        destination,
        mappedData,
        operation,
      );

      await emitSqlEvent(
        this.customLogger,
        context,
        this.eventEmitter,
        cachedDestination,
        cachedMappedData,
        operation,
      );
    }

    // Clear cache after both parts are processed
    operationInfo.name = 'Delete state';
    await execAndLog(
      this.customLogger,
      context,
      () => this.daprClient.state.delete(redisStore, cacheKey),
      operationInfo,
      operationDetails,
    );
  } catch (error) {
    this.customLogger.error(
      `Error in processing outbound: ${error.message}`,
      context,
      error.stack,
    );
    await moveToDeadLetterQueue(
      this.customLogger,
      context,
      redisStore,
      this.daprClient,
      cacheKey,
      message,
      MESSAGE_ACTION.GETORDERID,
    );
  } finally {
    if (release) {
      release();
    }
    this.customLogger.debug(`Released lock for ${cacheKey}`, context);
  }
}

Investigate and resolve topic consumption issue caused by multiple restarts in PROD-DI and resulting data loss
description:
🧠 Issue Analysis – Dapr Binding Retry Warning

🔍 Problem:

The Dapr sidecar logs the following warning intermittently for high-frequency EventHub bindings: 

Error processing EventHubs events for topic <topic>. Error: %!v(MISSING). Retrying...

This typically happens when:

  • The application does not respond successfully to Dapr after receiving a message.

  • Dapr interprets this as a failure, so it retries the same message (based on EventHub retry semantics).

🧩 Root Cause:

In the existing start() method, the server.binding.receive(...) handlers call this.handleMessage(...) without awaiting the async function.

Since the handler is asynchronous, not awaiting it causes the handler to return a resolved Promise immediately, regardless of the actual processing outcome. Dapr considers the request as failed if:

  • The process throws internally.

  • Or, more importantly in this case: the handler returns before the async logic finishes, which can lead to unacknowledged messages.

This becomes problematic with high-throughput EventHub topics, where messages are pushed rapidly and Dapr expects strict and consistent handling.

✅ Resolution:

All this.handleMessage(...) calls in binding handlers have been updated to use await. This ensures:

  • The app only signals success to Dapr after the message has been fully handled.

  • Avoids false negatives and unnecessary retries by Dapr.

  • Reduces back-pressure, especially when the system is under load.


In testing the impact of the new changes with big load of data

titre: Comparaison: PostgreSQL vs. SQL Server
description:
Category

PostgreSQL

SQL Server (MSSQL)

Notes / Comments

General Syntax

ANSI-compliant, strict on standards

ANSI-based, with many proprietary extensions

PostgreSQL is more open-source standard driven.

String Type

TEXT, VARCHAR(n), CHAR(n)

VARCHAR(n), NVARCHAR(n), CHAR(n)

PostgreSQL TEXT has no length limit; SQL Server distinguishes between Unicode types.

Integer Type

SMALLINT, INTEGER, BIGINT

TINYINT, SMALLINT, INT, BIGINT

SQL Server has TINYINT, which PostgreSQL lacks.

Decimal / Numeric

NUMERIC, DECIMAL(p,s), REAL, FLOAT

DECIMAL(p,s), NUMERIC(p,s), FLOAT, REAL

Mostly similar, though precision handling may differ slightly.

Boolean Type

BOOLEAN (true/false)

No native BOOLEAN; uses BIT (0/1)

PostgreSQL supports native boolean type.

Date/Time Types

DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP, INTERVAL

DATE, TIME, DATETIME, DATETIME2, SMALLDATETIME

SQL Server supports more granular control via DATETIME2.

UUID Support

UUID (native)

UNIQUEIDENTIFIER

PostgreSQL has native UUID functions and extensions.

Binary Type

BYTEA, Large Object (LOB)

BINARY(n), VARBINARY(n), IMAGE (deprecated)

PostgreSQL uses BYTEA; no direct length-based binary.

Binary Type

BYTEA (no length attribute supported)

BINARY(n), VARBINARY(n) (length required)

✅ PostgreSQL does not support a length constraint on BYTEA.
❌ TypeORM will throw an error if you define length with BYTEA.
⚠️ In SQL Server, length is required for BINARY and optional (default to 1) for VARBINARY if unspecified.

JSON Support

JSON, JSONB (binary)

NVARCHAR(MAX) + JSON_VALUE, OPENJSON

PostgreSQL has native, indexed JSON support (JSONB).

Arrays

Native array support: INTEGER[], etc.

Not supported natively

PostgreSQL allows array columns with rich operators.

Auto-Increment / Identity

SERIAL, BIGSERIAL, GENERATED

IDENTITY, SEQUENCE

PostgreSQL SERIAL is shorthand for SEQUENCE; modern way uses GENERATED.


Upsert Support

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE

MERGE or IF EXISTS ... UPDATE

PostgreSQL is more concise and powerful.

Parameter Passing (SQL)

$1, $2, etc. (positional)

@param (named)

PostgreSQL uses positional parameters in prepared statements.

Stored Procedures / Functions

FUNCTION, PROCEDURE, DO $$

PROCEDURE, FUNCTION

SQL Server separates procedures and functions clearly.

Limit / Offset

LIMIT x OFFSET y

OFFSET y ROWS FETCH NEXT x ROWS ONLY

PostgreSQL is simpler; SQL Server uses SQL:2008 syntax.

Licensing

Open-source (PostgreSQL License)

Commercial (Microsoft EULA)

PostgreSQL has no licensing cost.

 

Identity Authentication

 

 

 

❌ No native support for Azure AD / Managed Identity in official Postgres drivers

✅ Supports Azure AD & Managed Identity using authentication

SQL Server (Azure) supports ManagedIdentityClientId for identity-based auth; PostgreSQL requires workarounds.

Migrating from InMemoryQueue to Redis SDK

 1. Current State
Your system is using two different mechanisms in different parts of the services:

InMemoryQueue:

Used in several services (e.g., mesx-master-data-ingestion, mesx-production-data-ingestion, mesx-shipment-data-ingestion, etc.) for queueing operations.

CacheManager:

Used in mesx-ewm-gateway-backend for caching.

Services using InMemoryQueue:

mesx-master-data-ingestion

mesx-production-data-ingestion

mesx-shipment-data-ingestion

mesx-plant-hierarchy-data-ingestion

mesx-order-data-ingestion

mesx-ewm-gateway-backend

Service using CacheManager:
mesx-ewm-gateway-backend: Uses CacheManager for caching, not for queuing.

 2. Challenges with InMemoryQueue
Scalability:

In-memory queues are local to each instance. As services scale horizontally, each instance maintains its own queue, leading to data inconsistency across instances. Redis provides a centralized queue that can be shared across multiple instances.

Durability:

In-memory queues lose all data when the app crashes or restarts, which is a risk in production systems. Redis queues support data persistence, meaning that data survives restarts and crashes.

Limited Inter-service Communication:

In-memory queues are not shared between services, limiting communication between distributed services. Redis, on the other hand, provides shared queues across multiple microservices, improving inter-service communication.

Lack of Advanced Features:

Redis provides advanced features such as retries, dead-letter queues (DLQs), message expiration, and monitoring, which are harder to implement with in-memory queues.

 3. Target State
The goal is to migrate the InMemoryQueue mechanism to a Redis-based queueing system for all services that use queues, except mesx-ewm-gateway-backend, which uses CacheManager for caching. Specifically, for mesx-ewm-gateway-backend, the InMemoryQueue part will be replaced with Redis, but the CacheManager remains untouched.

 4. Why Migrate to Redis SDK?
Redis SDK for Queueing is favored for several reasons:

Scalability:

InMemoryQueue cannot scale effectively because each instance has its own queue. Redis provides a centralized, shared queue, which is accessible across multiple services and instances.

Durability:

In-memory queues lose all messages if the application restarts. Redis ensures message persistence, offering better reliability and data retention across crashes.

Inter-service Communication:

Redis-backed queues allow multiple services to interact with the same queue, improving distributed processing and communication between microservices.

Advanced Features:

Redis supports dead-letter queues, message retries, and TTL for messages, which are not easily achievable with in-memory queues.

Monitoring & Observability:

Redis provides tools to monitor queue lengths, message processing rates, and errors, improving operational visibility and debugging.

Performance:

Redis is highly performant and can handle millions of messages per second, making it ideal for high-throughput systems.

mesx-ewm-gateway-backend - No Changes Needed
The mesx-ewm-gateway-backend service currently uses CacheManager for caching (not for queuing).

No change is required for this service because the migration to Redis only impacts queueing, not caching.

The CacheManager will continue to handle in-memory caching for synchronizing data like WorkCenters, Materials, and Storage Locations.

For the rest of the services, we'll replace InMemoryQueue with Redis, while keeping the CacheManager logic for mesx-ewm-gateway-backend intact.

Updated initializeQueues() Method Using Redis (mesx-ewm-gateway-backend)
Here’s how we could modify your initializeQueues() method to use Redis for queuing instead of the in-memory queue. The main idea is that after loading the queues, we will push them to Redis instead of to the in-memory queue.

Investigate events reprocess from event hub
description:
We are currently using Dapr bindings to consume high-throughput messages from Azure Event Hub. These messages are critical for downstream processes such as updating services, syncing data, or triggering business workflows.

Recently, we’ve encountered issues where Dapr intermittently logs warnings like:

“Error processing EventHubs events for topic <topic>. Retrying…”

What’s Really Happening

The warnings occur because our application either:

  • Does not acknowledge the message in time, or

  • Fails silently due to async handler issues or runtime crashes.

As a result:

  • Dapr assumes the message failed to process.

  • It retries the same message, possibly multiple times.

  • This can cause:

    • Message duplication

    • Performance degradation

    • Delayed downstream actions

    • Data inconsistencies

users might see delayed updates, or incorrect system behavior.


What We Want to Achieve

We want a resilient message reprocessing strategy that:

  1. Detects and handles failed or missed messages

  2. Ensures messages are processed exactly once

  3. Reduces operational risk and customer-facing impact

Proposed Strategy: Reprocessing 

1. Track What We’ve Successfully Handled

We'll log every message that was successfully processed  using a unique message ID or sequence number  into a reliable storage (e.g. Redis or Cosmos DB).

This creates a source of truth to compare against incoming Event Hub messages.

2. Detect What We Missed

We’ll build a detection mechanism that:

  • Pulls messages from Event Hub over a recent time window

  • Compares them to our “success log”

  • Flags the messages that were never processed

Think of it as a reconciliation process between “what we got” vs. “what we handled”.

3.Safely Reprocess Only What’s Needed

A scheduled task (e.g. with NestJS scheduler) will:

  • Pull the unhandled messages

  • Run them through our normal processing logic

  • Skip any already-processed ones using ID checks

This guarantees:

  • No duplicates

  • No lost events

  • No manual intervention

Next Steps (after validation)

  1. Define the tracking schema and store (Cosmos DB or Redis, etc...).

  2. Implement a reprocessing scheduler/job in NestJS.

  3. Test under simulated high-throughput scenarios.

titre: Testing the Impact of await in dapr receive in prod di
description:
🧠 Issue Analysis – Dapr Binding Retry Warning

🔍 Problem:

The Dapr sidecar logs the following warning intermittently for high-frequency EventHub bindings: 

Error processing EventHubs events for topic <topic>. Error: %!v(MISSING). Retrying...

This typically happens when:

  • The application does not respond successfully to Dapr after receiving a message.
  • Dapr interprets this as a failure, so it retries the same message (based on EventHub retry semantics).

🧩 Root Cause:

In the existing start() method, the server.binding.receive(...) handlers call this.handleMessage(...) without awaiting the async function.

Since the handler is asynchronous, not awaiting it causes the handler to return a resolved Promise immediately, regardless of the actual processing outcome. Dapr considers the request as failed if:

  • The process throws internally.
  • Or, more importantly in this case: the handler returns before the async logic finishes, which can lead to race conditions or unacknowledged messages.

This becomes problematic with high-throughput EventHub topics, where messages are pushed rapidly and Dapr expects strict and consistent handling.

✅ Resolution:

All this.handleMessage(...) calls in binding handlers have been updated to use await. This ensures:

  • The app only signals success to Dapr after the message has been fully handled.
  • Avoids false negatives and unnecessary retries by Dapr.
  • Reduces back-pressure, especially when the system is under load.

💡 Note:

Although the system seemed to “work” at a glance, this underlying issue can:

  • Cause message duplication under high frequency.
  • Lead to performance degradation if retries pile up.
  • Mask real errors in Dapr logs due to %!v(MISSING) unformatted error.

Analysis - Data Reconciliation between source and MES X.0 following dapr crash
description:
Context :

In our current architecture, we're using Dapr for event-driven communication. Events are handled by our NestJS-based ingestion microservice. As it stands, the microservice:

  • Publishes events through Dapr's pub/sub system.

  • Temporarily stores events in memory during processing.

  • Includes a beforeShutdown hook that writes to a json file but this mechanism is not fully reliable or consistent as it's currently not working as it should

The Problem

The current mechanism introduces a critical reliability issue:

  • When Dapr crashes or restarts, any events stored in memory are lost.

  • If the service crashes unexpectedly or the container is force-stopped, the beforeShutdown logic is not guaranteed to run, meaning unprocessed events are never persisted.

  • This leads to data discrepancy and incomplete event flows, which is unacceptable in a production setup.

What We’re Trying to Solve

We need to ensure that no events are lost, even if Dapr or the ingestion service goes down. We want a system that can detect unprocessed events, and once Dapr is back up, replay or process them automatically closing the reliability gap.


Proposed Solution

To address this issue, I’m proposing the following changes:

     1. Move from In-Memory to Redis for Event Buffering

As a first step of the correction, instead of keeping events in memory, we'll store them in Redis:

  • Before sending an event to Dapr, it gets stored in Redis under a pending-events list or a similar structure that we should define later

  • Once the event is successfully processed , we remove it from Redis.

  • If the publish process, the event remains stored and safe for retry.

This gives us durability and crash resilience, which in-memory storage can’t offer.


    2. Introduce a Separate Correction Job

We'll create a dedicated service/job, completely decoupled from the ingestion service. This job will:

  • Periodically check Redis for any unprocessed events.

  • Check if Dapr is back and healthy.

  • If Dapr is available, it will re-process the events, then remove them from Redis.

  • If Dapr is still down, it will skip and retry later.

This way, data correction becomes a standalone, autonomous process that runs independently of the ingestion flow.


    3. Handle Dapr Health Checks

By default, the Dapr health endpoint (/v1.0/healthz) is only accessible from within the sidecar container.

So, for the recovery job to access this:

  • It needs to be in the same network as the Dapr sidecar, or

  • We give it its own Dapr sidecar instance, or

  • It exposes an external endpoint so that our correction job/service can access it (not sure if possible)

  • @MISSAOUI Chedy (external) Should tell is what is the best approach

This check will prevent us from retrying events prematurely and reduce the risk of failed retries.

titre: Use dynamic configuration using push refresh - Analysis
description:
📘 Dynamic Configuration: Push Refresh Analysis

🧩 Background

Our goal is to dynamically manage runtime configuration using Azure App Configuration, enabling updates without restarting containers.

🔁 Pull-Based Refresh

This method uses a cache with TTL (Time-To-Live):

  • The app reads config values from Azure App Configuration and caches them.

  • When the TTL expires, the app fetches fresh values.

✔️ Pros

  • Simple to implement.

  • No extra Azure components needed.

❌ Cons

  • Changes aren't immediate — you must wait for TTL to expire.

  • Not suitable for dynamic features that require real-time control (e.g., toggles).

📡 Push-Based Refresh with Azure App Configuration Events

To eliminate latency, we analyzed Azure App Configuration’s Events feature.

🔔 How It Works

  1. Go to Azure App Configuration → Events.

  2. Enable "Event publishing".

  3. Set Event Hub as the event handler.

    • When a key or label changes, Azure sends an event to the configured Event Hub namespace & topic.

  4. Our application subscribes to the Event Hub.

    • On receiving the event, the app triggers an immediate configuration refresh using the SDK.


✔️ Benefits

  • Instant propagation of config changes.

  • No need to poll or rely on TTLs.

  • Scalable and event-driven.

🛠️ Example Use Case

Let’s say we enable/disable a feature flag (UNS_ENABLED). With push refresh:

  • Azure emits an event within seconds.

  • Our app picks it up and applies the new value immediately, without restart or delay.

✅ Conclusion & Next Steps

The push method using Azure App Configuration + Event Hub offers a robust, real-time refresh mechanism, solving the limitations of the TTL-based pull approach.

🔧 Action:

We recommend moving forward with testing the push-based setup in our environment to confirm:

  • Event delivery reliability

  • Instant config refresh behavior

  • Integration stability

Once validated, this approach could be adopted as our standard for dynamic config management.

Design Solution on Cross browser authentication
description:
To work around Ping Federate's limitation of issuing only one refresh token at a time, the web application should manage its own session using the NestJS application's session mechanism, rather than relying on bearer tokens. 
The identity provider is used only for authenticating the user; once authenticated, the application manages user data through sessions as a stateful application.

The schema below recap the workflow:




Below the key point to implement the logic.

Authentication Framework
The application uses OpenID Connect protocol identity provider for authentication.
This is implemented using the openid-client library which provides OIDC client capabilities.

Session Management
Session Setup: The application uses Express sessions configured in main.ts:
Domain Configuration: The cookie domain is dynamically set based on environment variables or hostname.

app.use( 
  session({
    store: <provide redis store config>
    secret: <KEY_SECRET>,
    resave: false,
    saveUninitialized: true,
    cookie: {
      maxAge: <COOKIE_LIFETIME>
      domain: <DOMAIN>,
      secure: <SECURE_COOKIE>
    },
  }),
);

Middleware
There is 2 middlewares to implements:
  • Middleware 1: 
    • Check if user is authenticated, if no:
      • Save the current path in session variable (req.session.pathBeforeLogin)
      • Trigger authentication flow by redirect user to /api/auth/login
    • Once authenticated:
      • Store user data (claims, email, name, ...) into req.session.userInfo
      • Store token expirationTime into req.session.token.expireAt (in epoch format)
      • refresh token is stored into redis where the key is defined in a unique way to identify user (example email address)
  • Middleware 2: 
    • Check if req.session.token.expireAt is about to expire, if yes it should trigger token refresh from AuthService.RefreshToken (described below)
Service
There is one AuthService to create that implements the following methods:
  • GetloginUrl: 
    • Generate code verifier, state 
    • Save code verifier and state into Redis
    • Use openid-client to generate the url that redirects to IDP
  • GetLogoutUrl:  
    • Retrieve the id_token from Redis
    • Use openid-client to generate logout url and set the parameter hint_id_token
  • RefreshToken:
    • Retrieve refresh_token from Redis that should be safe_read
    • Use openid-client to retrieve refreshed  token from IDP
    • Save user data like name, mail, claims, ... into req.session.userInfo
    • Update redis with new refresh_token, id_token in safe_write way
  • HandleCallback
    • Use openid-client to retrieve callback data
    • Check code verifer and state
    • Delete code verifier and state (saved during GetloginUrl) from Redis
    • Update redis with new refresh_token, id_token in safe_write way
    • Save user data like name, mail, claims, ... into req.session.userInfo
    • Save new expirationTime in req.session.token.expireAt
Controller
Implements:
  • GET /api/auth/login that will call AuthService.GetloginUrl and redirect user to generated url
  • GET /api/auth/callback that will AuthService.HandleCallback and redirect user to req.session.pathBeforeLogin
  • GET /api/auth/logout that will call req.session.destroy then call AuthService.GetlogoutUrl

description:
we've encountered an issue with our pipeline linting rules related to the usage of quasar internal classes specifically those that use double underscores (like .q-field__control, .q-btn__content, and .q-item__section ). 

our current Stylelint configuration enforces kebab-case  naming for class selectors, which causes errors when using valid quasar classes that follow the BEM convention.

Since these classes are defined by the Quasar framework and are necessary in certain UI cases like for deep styling or targeting internal elements, we cannot rename or avoid them. As a result, this is blocking the pipeline unnecessarily.

target is to adjust the linting rules to allow BEM style selectors allowing '__' and '--' to avoid false positives while still enforcing our custom naming standards.

description:
Summary of the Trigger-Based Solution for Picking Order Updates

We implemented two SQL Server triggers to automatically update the picking_order table whenever changes occur in related tables:

  • trg_update_picking_order_rescheduler_wk_history: Updates picking_order when a record in rescheduler_wk_history is updated.

  • trg_update_picking_order_alert: Updates picking_order when a record in alert is updated.

Each trigger:
✅ Updates timestamps (updated_at, rescheduler_wk_history_updated_at, alert_updated_at) in picking_order automatically.
✅ Ensures consistency between picking_order and related tables without requiring additional queries in application code.

Why Triggers Are a Better Choice than TypeORM Listeners or Manual Updates

1️⃣ Compared to TypeORM Listeners

TypeORM offers event listeners/hooks (@AfterUpdate, @BeforeUpdate) that could track updates in rescheduler_wk_history and alert and manually update picking_order.

🔴 Drawbacks of TypeORM Listeners:

  • Application-Level Overhead: Runs in the application layer, increasing processing time.

  • Potential Data Inconsistency: If the app crashes mid-transaction, the update to picking_order might not happen.

  • Complex Dependency Management: Requires ensuring the right repository/service is injected for updates.

✅ Why Triggers Are Better:

  • Runs directly at the database level, ensuring updates happen instantly and atomically.

  • No need for extra database calls from the application.

  • Works even if the application goes down or restarts.

2️⃣ Compared to Manual Updates in Code

We could also update picking_order manually in the application code whenever rescheduler_wk_history or alert is updated.

🔴 Drawbacks of Manual Updates:

  • Extra Query Execution: Every update in rescheduler_wk_history or alert requires a separate update query for picking_order.

  • Risk of Missing Updates: If the developer forgets to add the update logic in all necessary places, picking_order can become outdated.

  • Concurrency Issues: If multiple updates happen at the same time, there’s a chance of race conditions leading to outdated data.

✅ Why Triggers Are Better:

  • Automatic and Reliable: Ensures updates happen consistently without needing extra logic in the app.

  • No Extra Queries: Reduces the number of queries executed by the application, improving efficiency.

titre: [Leveling-processor] - Analysis : Show WKs which are still in the buffer.
description:
📝 Feature: Process Buffer WKs in CosmosDB

📘 Description

We want to enhance our existing processing pipeline to also handle Work Centers (WKs) from the buffer table not just from the picking_order table.

The goal is to:

  • Process and display buffer WKs that meet certain criteria (buffer_status = 'RECEIVED' and 'IN PROGRESS')

  • Ensure they are differentiated from picking_order WKs in Cosmos

  • Avoid overwriting or mixing data

This change will make buffer WKs visible on the Leveling Board while ensuring data consistency, freshness, and easy filtering.

🔧 Technical Details

1.  Filtering Logic

  • Only include rows where buffer_status = 'RECEIVED' and 'IN PROGRESS'.

  • For each orderId, keep only the latest row based on updated_at (desc).


2.  Field Mapping: Buffer Table → picking_order (Cosmos)

  • picking_order (Cosmos) id → Use a prefixed value like buffer::{orderId}
    (To avoid collision with existing picking_order IDs)

  • picking_order (Cosmos) pickingOrderId → Maps to orderId from buffer

  • picking_order (Cosmos) plant → Maps to plant

  • picking_order (Cosmos) workcenter → Maps to productionLine

  • picking_order (Cosmos) tpaNumber → Maps to tpaNumber

  • picking_order (Cosmos) sourceLocation → Maps to sourceLocation

  • picking_order (Cosmos) destinationLocation → Maps to destinationLocation

  • picking_order (Cosmos) outbound → Maps to deliveryNumber

  • picking_order (Cosmos) qtyToBuild → Maps to quantity

  • picking_order (Cosmos) material → Maps to materialNumber

  • picking_order (Cosmos) plannedStartDate → Maps to startPickingDateTime

  • picking_order (Cosmos) sourceType → Set as constant 'buffer'
    (Used to distinguish buffer entries from picking_order ones)

3. CosmosDB Handling

  • Keep plant as the partition key

  • Add a new field sourceType = 'buffer' to distinguish documents

4. ORDER-API :

  • New function in orderApi: fetchReceivedBufferWks(plant,estimatedDate)

  • We should get only the most recent entry per orderId with buffer_status = 'RECEIVED' and 'IN PROGRESS'

5. Processor :

  • Add a new call similar to fetchOrdersByDate, but for buffer WKs

  • Map the buffer format to the Cosmos structure

  • Insert/update them using prefixed ID and sourceType

  • Periodically check and remove WKs that their buffer_status changes to 'ERROR' or 'SUCCESS'

  • In case we have duplicated WKs ( picking and buffer ) we need to keep the one from picking. (To be checked).

description:
🔍 Analysis: Kitting Flow

The current flow involves a series of validation and data-matching steps when processing a transfer operation within the kitting context:

  1. Transfer Operation Validation

    • The transfer must have a poka_yoke value of either API_L, API_P, or API_K.

    • The created_by field must be System. (Note: Verification of created_by is pending confirmation from @JEBALI Hiba .)

  2. Material Validation

    • The material associated with the transfer must be flagged as a kit material.

    • This is determined by checking the kitmat column (expected to be 1) in the material_dtl table located in the ORD domain.

  3. Destination Work Center (WC) Identification

    • The destination_wc is retrieved from the picking_order table (also in the ORD domain).

    • To identify the correct WK(s), the following criteria must be satisfied:

      • The material in the picking_order matches the material in the transfer.

      • The D_TRANSFERRED_QUANTITY in picking_order (requires ingestion into MES) matches the transfer quantity.

      • The timestamp window for matching is a ±30-second range around the updated_at value of the transfer.
        (This range will be reviewed and fine-tuned to ensure optimal accuracy.)

      • The destination_wc must not be null.

      • The custom_status field must be empty.

      • transfer_id = null

  4. Handling Multiple WK Matches

    • If multiple WKs satisfy all criteria, the system should select the one with the latest updated_at timestamp (TOP 1 ORDER BY updated_at DESC).

✅ Planned Actions

📌 Service Affected: ewm-gateway-be

📌 Target Module: sendEventTransfer method

🔧 Implementation Steps

1. Transfer Eligibility Validation

Update the logic in sendEventTransfer to include validation against the following criteria:

  • The poka_yoke field must be one of: API_L, API_P, or API_K.

  • The created_by field must be set to "System".

  • The associated material must be marked as a kit material (flagged as kitmat).

2. Destination Work Center (via order-api)

Create a new query to retrieve the appropriate destination_wc  from the picking_order table, based on the following matching logic:

  • Match Conditions:

    • material in picking_order matches the material from the transfer (the material from the transfer will be passed at the body of the endpoint)

    • transfered_quantity in picking_order equals the transfer’s quantity (the transfer's quantity will be passed at the body of the endpoint)

    • plant in picking order equals the transfer's plant.

    • custom_status must be empty.

    • destination_wc must not be null.

    • The updated_at timestamp from picking_order must fall within a ±30-second range around the updated_at value of the transfer.
      (Note: This window will be reviewed and adjusted for optimal precision.)

  • Ordering & Selection:

    • Return TOP 1 record ordered by updated_at DESC.

3. Database Schema Update

  • Add a new column to the picking_order table:

    • Column name: transfered_quantity

    • Type: number

    • Constraints: nullable = true

  • Data Source: Populate this new column by ingesting data from the D_TRANSFERRED_QUANTITY field of the S_PICKING_ORDER table.


🔍 Analysis: Auto-Replenishment Flow 

The current auto-replenishment process includes a sequence of validation steps and data-matching logic to correctly handle transfer operations. The flow can be broken down into the following stages:

1. Transfer Operation Validation

To qualify as an auto-replenishment transfer, the following conditions must be met:

  • The poka_yoke field in the transfer record must be equal to API_P.

  • The created_by field must be set to System.

2. Material Eligibility Check

The material associated with the transfer must be marked as auto-transfer.
This is determined by validating the material in the material_dtl table within the MSTR domain:

  • The auto_transfer column must be set to 1.

3. Destination Work Center (WC) Identification

To determine the appropriate destination work center:

  • Introduce a new table in the transfer-api domain named:
    components_for_replenish, with the following schema:

    • plant (INT, length: 4, NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY)

    • material (NVARCHAR, length: 18, NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY)

    • workcenter (NVARCHAR, length: 8, NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY)

  • This table will be ingested from [MES_FAURECIA].[dbo].[COMPONENTS_FOR_REPLENISH] in the transfer-di service, where:

    • plant maps to PLANT

    • material maps to COMPONENT

    • workcenter maps to WORKCENTER

🔗 Matching Logic:

To determine the destination_wc, match records from the components_for_replenish table using the following criteria:

  • material matches the transfer’s material

  • plant matches the transfer’s plant

  • The transfer’s updated_at timestamp is within a ±30-second window of the components_for_replenish record (subject to refinement for accuracy)

⚖️ Handling Multiple Matching Work Centers

If multiple work centers match all the criteria:

  • Select the work center with the most recent updated_at 
    (TOP 1 ORDER BY updated_at DESC)

✅ Planned Actions:

📌 Affected Service: ewm-gateway-be

📌 Target Method: sendEventTransfer method

🔧 Implementation Steps

1. 🔍 Transfer Eligibility Validation

Enhance the sendEventTransfer logic to validate transfer records using the following criteria:

  • poka_yoke must be exactly API_P.

  • created_by must be set to "System".

  • The associated material must be flagged as an auto-transfer material (i.e., auto_transfer = 1).

2. 📥 Destination Work Center (transfer-api)

Develop a query in transfer-api to resolve the appropriate destination_wc (workcenter) using the new components_for_replenish table.

🎯 Matching Conditions:

  • plant must match the transfer’s plant.

  • The updated_at timestamp of the components_for_replenish record must fall within ±30 seconds of the transfer.updated_at timestamp.

    (This time window will be revisited for optimal precision.)

🧩 Selection Logic:

titre: [COM] Analysis - Standardize timezone management
description:
📘 Analysis – Frontend-Based Timezone Conversion Strategy

🎯 Objective
After discussions, we have rejected the backend-based timezone conversion approach to avoid unnecessary computation and loops on the server side.
Instead, the decision is to handle timezone conversion entirely on the frontend, improving performance and simplifying backend logic.

A new timezone utility function will be implemented in the frontend common library (mesx-commonlib) to handle this conversion in a consistent and maintainable way.

⚙️ Current State

  • All timestamps are correctly stored in UTC in the backend/database.

  • Timezone conversion is inconsistently applied:

    • The frontend uses different libraries like Intl, moment, and Luxon.

    • The backend also contains scattered formatting logic using toLocalTime(), date-fns, or Luxon.

⚠️ Problems With the Current Approach

  • Redundant conversion logic across frontend and backend.

  • Inconsistent display of dates across different modules and teams.

  • Increased maintenance cost due to duplicate logic.

  • Unnecessary server load if conversion is done during bulk operations in the backend.

  • Risk of double conversion or wrong formatting.

🚫 Why We Rejected the Backend-Based Proposal

  • Backend formatting requires extra data transformation and looping, which adds overhead and complexity.

  • Backend should focus on business logic and data — not UI concerns like formatting.

  • Centralizing in the backend limits flexibility on the frontend side (e.g., if formatting needs differ across views).

  • Passing timezones through request headers (X-Plant-Timezone) is not accessible on the frontend, making it impractical for rendering.

✅ New Solution – Frontend Timezone Conversion

We will shift all timezone conversion responsibilities to the frontend. The backend will continue sending raw UTC timestamps, and the frontend will handle:

  • Converting timestamps to the plant-local or user-local timezone.

  • Formatting dates according to application needs (e.g., yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss or ISO).

A shared utility function will be created in mesx-commonlib/utils/timezone.js for consistent usage across all components.

🔧 Utility Function Example 

formatUtcToLocalTime(utcDate: string, timezone: string, formatStr?: string): string

  • utcDate: A UTC timestamp string.

  • timezone: A valid IANA timezone string (e.g., "Europe/Berlin", "Africa/Tunis").

  • formatStr: Optional format string (e.g., 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm').

📁 Location

mesx-commonlib/utils/timezone.js

📦 Example Usage 

import { formatUtcToLocalTime } from 'mesx-commonlib/utils/timezone.js';

const plantTimezone = 'Africa/Tunis'; // Can be loaded from config, user settings, etc.
const localTime = formatUtcToLocalTime(order.createdAt, plantTimezone);

🧱 Design Highlights

FeatureDescription
🧠 Centralized Logic One reusable utility function in the frontend common library.
⚙️ Lightweight No backend overhead, reducing server load.
🌍 Flexible Timezones Uses IANA timezones; plant timezone can come from app config or user profile.
🖼️ Custom Formatting Developers can specify custom output formats (ISO, short, readable, etc.).
🚫 No Header Usage Does not rely on X-Plant-Timezone; purely frontend-side.

🔄 Migration Plan

StepAction
1️⃣ Implement formatUtcToLocalTime() in mesx-commonlib/utils/timezone.js.
2️⃣ Identify all frontend usages of moment, Intl, or Luxon.
3️⃣ Replace existing logic with the new utility.
4️⃣ Ensure backend continues sending raw UTC timestamps only.
5️⃣ Define how the frontend retrieves the plant timezone (config/user data).
6️⃣ Audit views for consistent formatting.
7️⃣ Document usage with code examples in the developer guide.

🧾 Audit Plan

We will perform a full audit of all frontend modules to:

  • Remove usage of deprecated or scattered timezone libraries (moment, raw Intl, etc.).

  • Standardize all formatting logic using the new common utility.

  • Verify visual consistency and correct output across all screens and plant timezones.

📌 Conclusion

By moving all timezone conversion to the frontend:

  • We reduce processing on the backend, improving performance and scalability.

  • We standardize formatting across all frontend views.

  • We gain more flexibility for user-based or plant-based formatting needs.

  • We simplify backend logic, allowing it to focus purely on business and data concerns.

This approach results in a cleaner, faster, and more maintainable MES architecture.

titre: Troubleshooting LVL processor issue
description:
The issue occurred on the processor level. When we checked the processor, we found that no task event had been received from the orchestrator.

Upon checking the orchestrator, it appeared to be running. However, the logs showed a restart at 5:00 AM. During the app initialization — specifically at the step where the orchestrator fetches the list of plants to create and dispatch tasks to the processor — a 500 Internal Server Error occurred: 

[Nest] 18 - 05/14/2025, 5:00:28 AM ERROR [JobsLoggerService] {"context":{"method": 
"startOrchestrator","service":"OrchestratorService","userId":"MESXSystem"}, 
"message":"Error schedulerInterval {\"error\":\"Internal Server Error\",\" 
error_msg\":\"{\\\"message\\\":\\\"Failed to retrieve data\\\",\\\"statusCode\ 
\\":500}\",\"status\":500}","timestamp":"2025-05-14T05:00:28.225Z"}

We also found a related issue on the same instance affecting the plt-hry API, which indicated a database-related error.

Additionally, by checking Redis, we confirmed that the last task was processed before the orchestrator




To unblock the situation, we manually restarted the orchestrator. For a long-term fix, we need to ensure that the orchestrator can reliably fetch the plant list during startup.
We continued the investigation into the database connection issue with Chedy's support and by informing Jacques

During the investigation of a production issue, I encountered a database connection error during the scale-up of a new replica of the API microservice: 

vbnetCopyEdit[Nest] 18 - 05/14/2025, 5:02:09 AM ERROR [TypeOrmModule] Unable to connect to the database. Retrying (5)...

This may cause issues for the invoker app calling the affected endpoint.

I looked into why this occurred, as we haven't seen this issue in other environments. After discussing it with Chedy and reviewing the DB metrics, we confirmed there were no signs of system failure or any database-related issues at that time. Chedy suggested it might be a network latency issue between the container and the database.

I investigated further and found that this error has occurred multiple times over the past 30 days (as shown in the attached screenshot). I also attempted to retrieve logs from one of the impacted replicas and didn't found relevant entries.

Since this might be related to network configuration or firewall settings, I wanted to inform jacques in case he has any insights. Additionally, this raises the question of whether disabling the firewall for the production environment could help avoid such issues in the future.

 
As a corrective action, Jacques requested the Cyber team to disable the firewall in the production environment.
We are waiting now for cyber team response

Analysis - Tagging Work Items on ppr and pro deployments 2
description:
Azure build pipelines has the capability to detect work items linked to the build by leveraging work item references in the version control commit messages.

This mechanism works well as long as builds are triggered based on branches and commits; and enables the usage of the Generate Release Notes (Crossplatform) plugin.

Unfortunately, previous work on #118781, highlighted that this mechanism does not work well on builds triggered via tags.

Related work items calculation for builds triggered via tags does not take into consideration previous tags and links all the work item available in the history of the repository which is not acceptable.

Options to determine work items related to release

Options 1: Use custom logic to determine work items

Based on work items linked in commit messages and latest vs current semantic version tags, implement script to determine work items related to a build.

Pros
  • Flexible mechanism
  • Fit for purpose
  • Related work item calculation repeatable
  • We get to release by simply tagging a commit
Cons
  • Implementation & maintenance effort

Options 2: Shift branching strategy to Git Flow and Rely on Pipelines Mechanism

If we rely on a separate release branch for releases, we can:
  • Release only from a release branch
  • Create a pipeline that take care of release actions including tagging
This way pipeline making the release is triggered from a branch + commit making the azure pipeline work item calculation usable.

Pros
  • Relying on available mechanism for related work item calculations
  • Leveraging Generate Release Notes (Crossplatform) plugin.
Cons
  • Big change to branching strategy
  • Release is now a multi-step process involving creating a pull request
  • Calculation not repeatable
  • Less flexibility

Given
  • Default cookie configuration in azure container app ( PR 87959: Default Cookie Configuration Easy Auth )
  • easyauth-ui vue application making request to the backend every 7 seconds, and stopping upon authentication error:
    https://dev.azure.com/faurecia-cloud/MES_X.0/_git/mesx-proto-easyauth/commit/b3e6b2fd17e3fd9c3fa21755873ccf8c35b630bc?refName=refs%2fheads%2fmain
When
  • Page is left opened for 24 hours
Then
  • Upon 8 hours we get an authentication error

  • Cookie max age is set to Session:
We conclude that rolling expiration is not enabled by default, in addition no signs of it being supported in the documentation.

Attempt 2: Background Token Refresh via EasyAuth token store config

Azure container apps easyauth allows to customize the underlying id token store and to specify a storage blob in which tokens and their related information are stored.

ARM Schema for configuring the token store contains an interesting property login.token.tokenRefreshExtensionHours

The idea in this attempt is to set token refresh extension lesser than the default lifetime of the ping federate token and to see whether cookie is refreshed along with the underlying token.
Given
  • token refresh is set to less than 1 hour
  • easyauth-ui vue application making request to the backend every 7 seconds, and stopping upon authentication error:
    https://dev.azure.com/faurecia-cloud/MES_X.0/_git/mesx-proto-easyauth/commit/b3e6b2fd17e3fd9c3fa21755873ccf8c35b630bc?refName=refs%2fheads%2fmain
When
  • Page is left opened for 1 hour
Then
  • Upon 1 hours, we get the authentication error:

Attempt 3: /.auth/refresh endpoint

When token store is enabled, the container app ingress exposes 2 endpoints:
  • GET https://mesx-dev.app.corp/.auth/me => to get current underlying token info
  • GET https://mesx-dev.app.corp/.auth/refresh => to refresh current underlying token
Idea here is if we refresh the token with /.auth/refresh then cookie will be refreshed as well.
Given
  • token store config is enabled (around line 406)
  • easyauth-ui vue application:
    • making request to the backend every 7 seconds
    • making request to /.auth/refresh every 10 minutes
    • stopping upon authentication error
When
  • Page is left opened for 1 hour
Then
  • Upon 1 hours, we get the authentication error:
