titre: [Analysis]: Design - Secure data access
description:
Current Problem Statement

There is a requirement to restrict data visibility on a per-plant basis. Each user should only be able to access and interact with the data corresponding to the plant(s) they are assigned to.

Approach 1: Retrieve and Parse Claims via Auth Endpoint

Mechanism:

  • Call the authentication service endpoint: mesx-dev.app.corp/ume-be/auth/claims.

  • This endpoint returns a list of group claims assigned to the current user.

  • From the group names, extract plant-specific identifiers. Example:

    • Group: WW_MII_GENERAL_TAR

    • SID extracted: TAR → corresponds to Plant 1146.

Frontend Integration:

  • In ume-ui, use a dedicated API to fetch all plants assigned to the user based on extracted SIDs.

  • Populate the dropdown list on the UI using only the plants the user is authorized for.

Admin Use Case:

  • Create an admin screen and backend endpoint that allows administrators to view which plants are assigned to each user (via SIDs).

  • Admins can manually verify or choose relevant plants per user using the same claims-based logic.

Pros:

  • Dynamic and centralized.

  • Leverages existing user-to-group mappings.

Approach 2: In-Memory Claims Caching

Mechanism:

  • Fetch and parse user claims only once per session upon the user’s first interaction (e.g., when opening the Downtime screen).

  • Cache the extracted plant SIDs in memory for the remainder of the session.

Usage:

  • For ume-ui, use the cached SIDs to determine which plants to display, reducing redundant network calls.

Pros:

  • Efficient runtime performance.

  • Reduces backend load and response latency.

Cons:

  • If user roles change mid-session, updates are not reflected unless the user logs out and back in.

Approach 3: Persistent Claims Storage with Manual Synchronization

Mechanism:

  • On first login or claims retrieval, persist the user's group claims to a table.

  • Provide a dedicated synchronization screen showing currently stored roles/claims.

  • If a user’s roles have been updated (e.g., new group added), the user can manually trigger a "Sync Roles" button to refresh the stored claims.

Frontend Usage:

  • Dropdown lists and screen-level authorizations are derived from stored claims rather than real-time parsing.

Pros:

  • Claims are persisted, reducing the need to call the auth service every time.

  • Offers transparency and control to the user over role synchronization.

Cons:

  • Requires additional development for UI and backend sync mechanism.

  • Manual intervention needed for role updates.

Approach 4: Manual Plant Assignment (Least Preferred)

Mechanism:

  • Build an admin screen where administrators manually assign plants to each user.

Usage:

  • Authorizations and UI dropdowns derive plant access from this manual mapping.

Pros:

  • Complete control over user-plant associations.

Cons:

  • Labor-intensive and error-prone.

  • Difficult to maintain and scale with large user bases.

  • Requires clear ownership: who is responsible for managing user-to-plant mapping?

titre: [PROD-DI] Investigate daprd issue - Health check not working as expected
description:
Regarding the issue related to the Dapr crash in the PPR environment on 05/06, we followed a structured investigation process:

  1. Alert Check: We started by checking whether any alerts were raised during that time, but none were found.

  2. Metrics Review: We reviewed the metrics related to replica restarts and found no restarts on that day.

  3. Log Analysis: We checked the logs and found no errors related to the prod-di service or any health probe failures. On the contrary, there were logs showing some events were received during that time.

  4. Restart Trace: The only restart observed was a manual one performed by Firas.

  5. Event Verification: We attempted to trace the events in Data Explorer and the CDC table, but since more than 7 days had passed (exceeding the retention period), we couldn't retrieve them.

Key Finding

The main concern now is the emergence of a new behavior we haven’t encountered before:

Dapr appears to be in a false state, where it continues receiving events in the container but stops functioning correctly.

Next Actions

  • If the issue occurs again, test the API's health probe first to check the actual status returned.

  • Verify that events are still present in both Data Explorer and the CDC table before restarting the container.

  • This will help us capture more accurate data and potentially identify the root cause of the issue.

titre: [ALerting] enhance the SMS sending logic
[Analysis]: Enhance Alert System to Avoid Redundant SMS Notifications per WK
description:
Following our recent meeting with @JEBALI Hiba, please find below my detailed analysis and proposal to enhance the alert system in order to prevent redundant SMS notifications per WK:

1. Data Model Enhancement – Alert Table

To support SMS notification tracking, four new boolean columns will be added to the ALERT table (by default false):

  • red_bell_sms

  • yellow_sms

  • orange_sms

  • red_sms

These columns will be updated once escalation occurs and the corresponding SMS has been sent. This will allow us to track which notifications have already been issued.

2. Alert Extraction & Data Transmission to MII

  • During alert extraction, relevant records will include the values of the newly added columns.

  • This enriched dataset will be transmitted to the MII transaction layer for processing and write-back operations.

3. Enhancing Logic in SC_MES_API/ALERT/TRANSACTION/V1/ALERT_AUTO_ESCALATE

We will update the transaction logic as follows:

  • Prior to triggering SMS sending, the system will check the values of the new SMS-related columns.

  • For example:

    • If escalate_level = YELLOW and yellow_sms = FALSE, the system will trigger the SMS notification.

    • If escalate_level = YELLOW and yellow_sms = TRUE, no SMS will be sent—only the alert update will proceed.

  • This logic applies similarly for RED, ORANGE, and RED_BELL escalation levels.

4. Post-MII Write-Back Updates

  • Upon successful MII write-back, the system will update the appropriate SMS flag (yellow_sms, red_sms, etc.) based on the alert’s escalation level.

  • This ensures that the state of each alert is clearly tracked and prevents duplicate SMS transmissions for the same alert condition.

5. Red Bell Alert Specifics

  • Red Bell alerts will be handled distinctly:

    • Only alerts with red_bell_sms = FALSE will be extracted.

    • Once processed, red_bell_sms will be updated to TRUE to avoid reprocessing.

  • Important: The current workaround involving updated_at filtering in the Red Bell query should be removed to ensure more reliable behavior based on the new flags.

6. SMS Handling at Alert Creation

  • As highlighted by @JEBALI Hiba, SMS management should also be integrated into the alert creation process.

  • The alert creation transaction will be updated to:

    • Send an SMS immediately upon creation.

    • Retrieve the most specific user configuration for the Production Supervisor role by prioritizing location types in the following order:
      PLC > WORKCENTER > PROD_LINE > UAP.

  • Note: This point can be addressed within this User Story or handled separately in a dedicated one. Please note that the associated workload is minimal

✅ Summary of Benefits

  • Elimination of redundant SMS notifications.

  • Improved traceability of alert escalations and notifications.

[Picking Screen] - HIGH - Manage Alerts for SFG Flow Analyse
description:
🔍 Developer Analysis – Alert Workcenter Assignment Logic (SFG_PIK Flow)

✅ Solution 1 – Dynamic Retrieval from Production Order (Accepted)

If the Workcenter (WK) status is before SFG_PIK_CLOSED (e.g., SFG_PIK_LAUNCHED, SFG_PIK_KITTING, SFG_PIK_PRODUCTION):

  • The alert should be created on the current workcenter of the related Picking Order (PIK).

  • This value must be fetched live from the PIK resource during alert creation, as the workcenter may change due to line updates.

📌 Implementation Logic:

  1. Take the current WK + Plant, query the picking order table → retrieve PIK number.

  2. With the PIK number and plant, query the production order table → retrieve the current workcenter.

  3. Use this workcenter for alert creation.

✅ This ensures the alert is always tied to the accurate, up-to-date workcenter — even in case of line changes.

❌ Solution 2 – Based on Upstream Line Columns (Rejected)

This solution proposed using the following fields:

  • D_PRODUCTION_LINE_UPSTREAM from S_PICKING_ORDER

  • SFG Flow config from the server configuration at plant level

Logic Summary:

  • If PRODUCTION_LINE_UPSTREAM is not null/empty AND SFG flow config = YES:

    • Compare the workcenter from the upstream line with the one from the production order.

    • If they match, use the upstream line’s workcenter.

    • Else, fall back to the production order workcenter.

  • In other cases, retain current behavior.

❗ Rejection Reason:

  • The two injected columns are not reliable for sourcing workcenter data.

  • Since we are already validating with the production order anyway, there's no added value in ingesting these additional columns.

  • Thus, this approach introduces unnecessary complexity without real benefit.

Here's your refined and complete write-up of Rule B – Post SFG_PIK_CLOSED Handling, incorporating all technical details and clarifying the architectural uncertainty:


🔁 Rule B – Post SFG_PIK_CLOSED Handling

Applies to: Both Solution 1 and Solution 2
Trigger: Workcenter (WK) status becomes SFG_PIK_CLOSED

✅ Behavior:

  • If an alert already exists:

    • Update the alert's workcenter (and PLC ID, if applicable) using the latest data from MES and MII.

  • If the alert does not exist:

    • Follow current alert creation rules (no change).

📌 Proposed Architecture (TBD between Pub/Sub and Job):

We are still evaluating whether to implement this logic via a Pub/Sub model or a scheduled/background job.

Option 1: Pub/Sub Approach

  • Publisher: Emits shop orders that transition into SFG_PIK_CLOSED during order data ingestion.

  • Subscriber: Picking Order module

    • Fetches all related alerts.

    • Updates workcenter and PLC ID fields using MES and MII data.

Option 2: Job-Based Approach

  • Scheduled/background job scans for orders in SFG_PIK_CLOSED.

  • Retrieves corresponding alerts and performs the same update logic as above.

🛠️ Additional Technical Requirements:

  • MII Write-Back Capability:

    • A new write-back mechanism to MII must be developed to allow updates to alert data.

    • Currently, no existing API or method supports alert updates in MII.

  • Alert Creation Logic Update:

    • Update the "create alert" function to align with Solution 1 logic.

    • Ensure newly created alerts immediately reflect the correct live workcenter based on the latest MES/MII data.

titre: [Order-API]: Data Model & APIs Enhancement – Alert Table
description:
1. Data Model Enhancement – Alert Table

To support SMS notification tracking, four new boolean columns will be added to the ALERT table (by default false):

  • red_bell_sms

  • yellow_sms

  • orange_sms

  • red_sms

These columns will be updated once escalation occurs and the corresponding SMS has been sent. This will allow us to track which notifications have already been issued.

2. Alert Extraction & Columns update

  • During alert extraction, relevant records will include the values of the newly added columns.

  • enhance the two endpoints: 

    fetchAlertsRedBell and 
    alertToBeEscalated

  • add new endpoint to update these columns (this API will take alert_id, plant, alert_level as inputs and based on the alert_level we will decide which column we will update, for example: if alert_level =YELLOW so we will update yellow_sms =true

5. Red Bell Alert Specifics

  • Red Bell alerts will be handled distinctly:

    • Only alerts with red_bell_sms = FALSE will be extracted.

    • Once processed, red_bell_sms will be updated to TRUE to avoid reprocessing.

  • Important: The current workaround involving updated_at filtering in the Red Bell query should be removed to ensure more reliable behavior based on the new flags.

titre: [MII]: Enhancing Logic in MII  transaction
description:
3. Enhancing Logic in SC_MES_API/ALERT/TRANSACTION/V1/ALERT_AUTO_ESCALATE

We will update the transaction logic as follows:

  • Prior to triggering SMS sending, the system will check the values of the new SMS-related columns.

  • For example:

    • If escalate_level = YELLOW and yellow_sms = FALSE, the system will trigger the SMS notification.

    • If escalate_level = YELLOW and yellow_sms = TRUE, no SMS will be sent—only the alert update will proceed.

  • This logic applies similarly for RED, ORANGE, and RED_BELL escalation levels.

titre: Review environment variables of type Boolean
description:
Hello team Everyone, 

During testing, I observed an issue related to environment variables of type boolean. Specifically, when a false boolean value is assigned to a configuration and later checked using a condition like !config.value as shown in the attached screenshot:

, it results in an unintended behavior — !false evaluates to true, causing the condition to incorrectly pass.

To address this, we’ve updated the requiredConfig structure to be an array of key-value pairs, where each key is a string and the value can be of type string | number | boolean | undefined : 

This change allows us to properly distinguish between missing and explicitly defined values.

With this update, we should revise our condition checks to explicitly validate whether the value is undefined rather than relying on truthy/falsy checks:

This approach prevents the issue from occurring when the value is explicitly set to false.

description:
New container app environment (cae2) characterized by a dedicated plan and VNET subnet with a larger IP range.

Target is to move existing container app resources with minimal downtime following this procedure:
  1. Deploy Dapr Resources to cae2
  2. Deploy API Services to cae2
  3. Ensure API Services start properly and are healthy
  4. Switch API Gateway to cae2
  5. Remove Active Services from cae1
  6. Create Active Services in cae2
  7. Ensure Active Services start properly and are healthy
  8. Remove all container apps from cae1
Note that this will create downtime at the data ingestion and materialized view level.

Update (31/07)

Low downtime move turns out to be too complex and error prone for the following reasons:
  • Tricky dependencies with container app volume references
  • Code duplication (terraform) that remain until all environments are aligned
  • Details must be changed in multiple places, especially challenging with duplicated code
Recommend to perform a downtime deployment which takes less time and is less error prone, with the following process:
  1. Disable all container app resources in the target environment
    1. Container apps
    2. Container app jobs
    3. Dapr resources
    4. Shared volumes references (under r-storage.tf)
  2. Change container app environment reference to new container app environment and re-introduce resources in the new cae in the following order (apply and validate for each step):
    1. Shared volumes references (under r-storage.tf) and 
      Dapr resources
    2. Passive container apps (api, backend, ui)
    3. App proxy and datahub
    4. Active Services (data ingestion and mv mechanisms)
    5. Container app Jobs & troubleshooting
    6. Enable alerts
New cae was missing firewall config to allow traffic to ping federate.

description:
✅ Current KPIs Available

The application currently supports 3 KPIs displayed on the UI:

  1. Received – Data not yet processed.

  2. Integrated – Data successfully integrated.

  3. Failed – Data integration failed.

✳️ Proposed New KPI: "Failed in Buffer"

Description:

This KPI will show entries that failed during the buffering stage, before integration even starts.

Condition:

Records where the buffer status is equal to "ERROR".

🧩 Scope of Change

1. Backend

  • A new condition will be added in the existing API to handle this KPI.

  • This ensures that when the user selects "Failed in Buffer", only relevant records are returned.

2. Frontend / User Interface

  • A new KPI badge/button labeled "Failed in Buffer" will be added next to the existing ones.

  • When selected, it will update the displayed data accordingly, just like other KPIs.

3. Export Functionality

  • The export feature will be updated to take this new KPI into account.

  • When "Failed in Buffer" is selected, only the relevant records will be exported.

In preparation for the production deployment of the user story related to enhancing SMS alert sending, here’s a summary of the required actions across the MES/MII components:

  • order-api:
    We will move to tag 1.21.0.
    ➤ Dependency check with Firas confirmed no impact, as the change involves adding a new endpoint, which is isolated.

  • order-data-ingestion:
    Target tag is 1.11.0, however, we encountered an issue.

Analyse the requirement to start developing the enhanced jobs
description:
Architectural Choices and Their Rationale:

  1. NestJS for Microservices: Chosen for its modular architecture, robust dependency injection, and enterprise-grade structure, which simplifies building scalable and maintainable microservices.

  2. Dapr Actors for Job Execution: Dapr Actors provide a powerful abstraction for managing individual, stateful job instances. Their "virtual actor" model, built-in state persistence (via Cosmos DB), and inherent fault tolerance (automatic activation, migration to healthy nodes, and persistent reminders) are critical for resilient job execution. This choice significantly reduces the complexity of implementing distributed state management and recovery logic manually.

  3. Cosmos DB for Persistence: Selected as the durable state store for both Dapr Actor state and the Scheduler Backend's job definitions and execution history. Its global distribution, elastic scalability, and transactional capabilities (within a partition) make it suitable for high-volume, stateful workloads.

  4. Dapr Reminders for Fault Tolerance and Scheduling: Reminders are the chosen mechanism for ensuring job continuity and periodic execution, as they are durably persisted and will reactivate an actor even after service restarts or deactivations. This is crucial for the "self-healing" aspect of the job system.

  5. Scheduler-Agent-Supervisor Pattern: This pattern provides a conceptual framework for the entire system.

    • The Scheduler Backend acts as the "Scheduler," orchestrating job workflows and initiating actor invocations.

    • The Job Microservices (Dapr Actors) serve as the "Agents," encapsulating the logic for individual job executions.

    • The Dapr Runtime (specifically the Placement service, State Management, and Reminders) inherently provides much of the "Supervisor" functionality, handling actor distribution, state persistence, and automatic recovery. An application-level supervisor component in the Scheduler Backend can complement this for higher-level workflow monitoring and compensation.

Proof of Concept (PoC) Plan:

The goal of the PoC is to validate the core interactions and Dapr Actor functionality.

  1. Dapr and Cosmos DB Setup:

    • Configure a Cosmos DB instance and a container for Dapr Actor state, ensuring actorStateStore: true in the Dapr component YAML.

    • Apply the recommended indexing policy optimization (excluding all but id and partitionKey) to the actor state container.

    • (Optional but recommended for larger state) Implement a basic application-level compression/decompression mechanism for actor state objects.

  2. Simple Job Service Microservice (Dapr Actor Host):

    • Create a basic NestJS application for the Job Service.

    • Define a simple Dapr Actor interface (e.g., ISimpleJobActor) as an abstract class.

    • Implement SimpleJobActor extending StatefulActor (or AbstractActor) and implementing ISimpleJobActor.

    • In SimpleJobActor:

      • Implement a method (e.g., executeJob(payload: any)) that saves some state (e.g., status: 'running') using setState and saveState.

      • Set a Dapr Reminder within executeJob to fire after a short duration (e.g., 30 seconds) to simulate a periodic check or delayed continuation.

      • Implement the receiveReminder callback to update the actor's state (e.g., status: 'completed') and then unregister the reminder.

    • Ensure the DaprServer starts before the NestJS app in main.ts.

    • Register SimpleJobActor in the NestJS module's providers.

  3. Basic Scheduler Backend Microservice:

    • Create a minimal NestJS application for the Scheduler Backend.

    • Inject DaprClient or DaprActorClient (if using @rayondigital/nest-dapr).

    • Create a controller endpoint (e.g., /schedule-simple-job) that:

      • Generates a unique Actor ID.

      • Invokes the executeJob method on an instance of SimpleJobActor using the Dapr client.

      • Records the job's initial state (e.g., Pending) in its own Cosmos DB JobExecutions collection.

  4. Demonstrate Fault Tolerance and Persistence:

    • Run both microservices.

    • Invoke the schedule-simple-job endpoint from the Scheduler Backend.

    • Observe the SimpleJobActor activating, saving state, and setting a reminder.

    • Crucially, restart the Job Service microservice.

    • Observe that after restart, the Dapr runtime reactivates the SimpleJobActor when its reminder fires, and the actor continues its execution from its last saved state, eventually unregistering the reminder and marking the job as complete.

    • Verify the state changes in Cosmos DB.

  5. Job Definition and History:

    • Implement basic CRUD operations for JobDefinition and JobExecutionHistory in the Scheduler Backend, persisting them to separate Cosmos DB containers with appropriate partition keys.

This PoC will provide a solid foundation and validate the core principles of your architecture before scaling up to more complex job scenarios.


This summary outlines key architectural decisions for Dapr Actor scheduling, persistence, and Azure Cosmos DB integration.

Why use Reminders, not Timers: Reminders are chosen for their durability, persisting across application restarts and actor deactivations. Unlike stateless timers, reminders are persisted using the Dapr actor state provider , ensuring reliable, long-running scheduled tasks. (Note: Centralized storage of reminders in the Dapr Scheduler service became the default in Dapr v1.15; in Dapr 1.13.6, they are primarily persisted via the configured actor state store.)  

How Scheduler Backend Interacts with Actors: The scheduler backend doesn't "create" actors directly. Instead, it sends a request to the Dapr actor service, specifying the actor's unique ID. The Dapr runtime, guided by the Placement service, routes the request to the correct host. If the actor is inactive, the runtime automatically activates it and rehydrates its state from the external store.  

Actor Revival on Shutdown/Restart: Upon shutdown or restart, in-memory actor objects are lost. However, because actor state (including reminder information) is durably persisted in Azure Cosmos DB, the Dapr runtime can activate a new actor instance and rehydrate its state from the database when a new request or reminder targets it, ensuring seamless continuity. Dapr's resiliency policies further enhance this by handling transient failures during operations.  

Deactivating Actors with Reminders: Reminders persist independently. They can be stopped by the actor explicitly unregistering them , by reaching a configured Time to Live (TTL) or invocation limit , or if the actor's state is explicitly deleted from the state store.  

Cosmos DB for State and History: Azure Cosmos DB serves as the unified state store:

Dapr Actor State (including Reminders): Stored in a dedicated Cosmos DB container, with Dapr automatically managing partition keys based on appId, actor type, and actor ID. The container's partition key must be   

/partitionKey.  

jobDefinitions Collection: Stores static job metadata, ideally partitioned by jobId or tenantId for efficient point reads.  

executionHistory Collection: Stores time-series execution logs. A composite partition key like /YYYY-MM-DD_jobId is recommended to distribute high write volumes and enable efficient time-range queries. Cosmos DB's native Time to Live (TTL) feature is used for automatic cleanup of old records.  

Co-location: jobDefinitions and executionHistory can reside in separate collections within the same Cosmos DB account, but direct cross-collection queries are not supported, requiring client-side aggregation.

[Analysis] Analysis of the Data Cleansing Job
description:
Create Two Endpoints in picking-be:

  1. /run-delete-picking-order-procedure
    This endpoint is responsible for initiating the data cleansing process for picking orders. It performs the following operations:

    • Calls the HRY domain service to retrieve the list of available plants.

    • Iterates through the retrieved plant list and, for each plant, calls the order-api's picking-order.controller endpoint, which executes the corresponding stored procedure.

    • Inputs passed to the procedure include:

      • The plant code.

    • The stored procedure will delete all picking orders with status CLOSED that are older than 3 months.

  2. /run-delete-production-order-procedure
    This endpoint triggers the data cleansing process for production orders and follows the same flow:

    • Retrieves the list of plants from the HRY domain.

    • Iterates through the list and calls the order-api’s production-order.controller endpoint for each plant, passing the required parameters.

    • Parameters:

      • The plant code.

      • The target stored procedure will delete production orders (piks) with status CLOSED that are older than 3 months.

  3. These two endpoints will be integrated into separate scheduled jobs responsible for data cleansing. The execution frequency of each job will be determined based on business priorities and system performance requirements.

[ANALYSIS] Prepare dataModel and technical analysis for Epart board use case
description:
Technical Analysis :


1. Initial Data Model Overview

As discussed with @JEBALI Hiba and @GHARMOUL Ahmed, I’ve drafted the initial data model for the Epart Board use case. Key tables involved are :


  • Shift Tracking: To track both the current and previous shifts.
  • Scrap List and Rework: To be filtered by plant, PLC, and shift.
  • Shift Details: Needed to track the upcoming (next) shift.
  • We’ve also extracted the relevant columns from each table based on screen requirements.

Below is a screenshot highlighting the tables required on the MES side for the Epart Board use case :

 

 

2. Epart Board Screen Breakdown

 

We reviewed the Epart Board screen  to map each screen element to its data source.

               Here is a Screenshot about the screen Epart Board :


 

  1. Field: Hour
  • Retrieved based on the values of DateShiftStart and DateShiftEnd and separated by an hour .

 

b. Field: Reference

  • Based on the part selection configuration in the resource config.
  • This configuration can have one of four values: sebango, tool, none.
  • We agreed that:
    • The MES side should ingest the part selection column in the resource table.
    • The open point is whether to include this table under the new ePart Board domain or use the existing Resource table in the Hierarchy domain.

 

c. Field: Target

  • Represents the sum of targets within a given shift.

 

d. Field: Production

  • Represents the sum of production within a given shift.

              e. Field: Delta

  • Calculated as the difference between total production and total target for the shift.

3. Fields Related to Non-TRS Use Case

The following fields are linked to the downtime-ticket system:

a. Cause

  • Determined by the min value of the cause of the  ticket:
    • If min ≥ 6: Display a red exclamation mark.
    • If min < 6: Display a grey circle.

b. Remark

  • Filled by counting the number of tickets that have remarks.

 

  1. Icon N
  • Allows the gap leader to switch between targets.
  • Not intended for operators.
  • If used to switch targets:
    • The master MII must be aware of this change.
    • Open question: Do we need writeback functionality to MII for this feature?

titre: Required Actions After Detecting Transaction Compatibility Issues
description:
Transactions with Compatibility Version Issues – Action Plan

Based on Task #126556

1 – Downtime Ticket Deletion

Transactions:

  • SC_MES_API/DOWNTIME/TRANSACTION/V1/DELETE_TICKET.trx

  • SC_MES_API/INTERFACE/DOWNTIME/V1/XCT_DELETE_TICKET.tqxc

Issue:
If MES is patched but MII is not, the latest encapsulated query will be missing, causing writeback failures for downtime ticket deletion.

Proposed Handling:

  • Check if MII returns an error indicating the transaction does not exist.

  • Alternatively, simulate pointing to a non-existent transaction to determine the exact error returned by MII.

  • If this error is detected, change the query path to use the previous direct deletion query:
    SC_MES_API/INTERFACE/DOWNTIME/V1/DELETE_TICKET.

2 – WK Kanban Update

Transaction:

  • SC_MES_API/WKINTEGRATION/TRANSACTION/V1/UPDATE_WK_KANBAN.trx

Issue:

  • If MES is patched but MII is not, XML structure changes on the MES side will cause failures.

  • If MII is patched but MES is not, the MES automatic WK integration endpoint will fail due to the same XML structure mismatch.

Proposed Handling:

  • Patch MES and MII simultaneously.

  • Alternatively, modify the MII transaction to:

    • Detect if the input XML matches the old structure → keep the old behavior.

    • Detect if it matches the new structure → use the updated logic.

3 – Work Center Update for SFG WK

Transactions:

  • SC_MES_API/INTERFACE/ALERT/V1/XCT_UPDATE_WC_FOR_SFG_WK.tqxc

  • SC_MES_API/ALERT/TRANSACTION/V1/TRX_UPDATE_WC_FOR_SFG_WK.trx

  • SC_MES_API/ALERT/QUERY/UPDATE_WC_FOR_SFG_WK.tqsq

Issue:
If MES is patched but MII is not, writeback failures occur for work center updates.

Proposed Handling:

  • Detect if MII returns an error indicating the transaction does not exist.

  • If detected, display a clear error message stating that this feature requires an MII patch.

4 – Alert Auto Escalate (Optional Action)

Transaction:
  • SC_MES_API/ALERT/TRANSACTION/V1/ALERT_AUTO_ESCALATE.trx

If needed, add explicit checks to verify the existence of the relevant fields.
This has been implemented and tested in a sandpit version to confirm correct handling of the new flags before performing any dependent checks.

[ANALYSIS] Secure retry for redis connection
description:
Heartbeat Mechanism and Redis Connection Enhancements

  1. Heartbeat Mechanism

  • Purpose:
    The heartbeat regularly sends a ping to the Redis server every 10 seconds to confirm that the connection is alive and responsive.

  • How it works:
    It uses the Redis PING command to check connection health. If the ping succeeds, the connection is healthy. If the ping fails due to authentication or connection errors (like an expired token or socket closure), the system triggers reconnection or token refresh.

  • Technical benefits:

    • Quickly detects silent or unexpected disconnections that might not raise explicit errors.

    • Prevents stale or broken connections from persisting.

    • Allows proactive recovery, reducing downtime and latency spikes.

  • Considerations:
    The 10-second interval balances timely failure detection with reasonable network and CPU usage. Heartbeat errors are logged and trigger recovery, but do not crash the system.

  1. Automatic Token Refresh with Managed Identity

  • Purpose:
    Azure Managed Identity tokens expire typically after an hour. Automatically refreshing the token ensures continuous Redis access without manual updates.

  • How it works:
    When connecting, the token and expiry time are retrieved. A timer schedules a refresh before expiry, which reconnects the Redis client using the new token.

  • Technical benefits:

    • Prevents downtime due to expired tokens.

    • Removes the need for static credential management.

    • Integrates securely with Azure AD, improving security.

  1. Exponential Backoff Retry Strategy

  • Purpose:
    Handles temporary errors like network glitches or throttling without flooding Redis or Azure with retries.

  • How it works:
    On failure, retries occur with gradually increasing delays (e.g., 100ms, 200ms, 400ms) up to a set maximum number of attempts.

  • Technical benefits:

    • Enhances success rates for reconnection or token refresh.

    • Minimizes load during partial outages.

  1. Safe Connection Recreation and Listener Management

  • Purpose:
    Ensures new Redis clients are created cleanly, preventing leftover event listeners or timers that cause memory leaks or inconsistent states.

  • How it works:
    Before creating a new client, existing listeners are removed and the old client is disconnected. New event listeners handle errors and recovery recursively.

  • Technical benefits:

    • Prevents accumulation of event listeners.

    • Reduces memory usage and unexpected behavior.

    • Guarantees a fresh client state after reconnecting.

  1. Timeout Wrapper for Promises

  • Purpose:
    Avoids operations hanging indefinitely during Redis commands or connection attempts.

  • How it works:
    Wraps asynchronous Redis operations with a timeout. If an operation exceeds the set time, it fails with a timeout error.

  • Technical benefits:

    • Prevents application freezing during network issues.

    • Enables quicker failure detection and recovery.

    • Keeps the system responsive under adverse conditions.

Summary

These combined improvements create a robust, secure, and self-healing Redis connection. The heartbeat mechanism continuously validates connection health. Automatic token refresh ensures uninterrupted secure access. Exponential backoff retries protect against temporary failures. Safe client recreation avoids memory leaks and inconsistencies. Finally, timeouts on operations prevent deadlocks, keeping the system stable and responsive.

titre: [eDashBoard] LayOut - Design epartboard screen
description:
As an operator, I want to use the Epartboard dashboard to monitor shift performance, track KPIs, and respond to alerts in real-time so that I can ensure efficient operations and quick decision-making.

Features & Functional Requirements

1. Shift Navigation

  • As a user, I want to navigate between different shifts (morning, afternoon, night) so I can view relevant data for each time period.

2. Tabs Navigation

  • As a user, I want to switch between tabs representing different KPIs so I can focus on specific performance areas.

3. Shift Tracking Details with Downtime Info

  • As a user, I want to see detailed shift tracking including downtime categorized by stoppage and unclassified duration so I can analyze production interruptions.

4. Picking Alerts

  • As a user, I want to view real-time alerts for picking issues so I can take immediate corrective actions.

5. Dynamic Widget Display for Right Part

  • As a user, I want the dashboard to dynamically display widgets based on the selected part so I can view relevant KPIs and metrics.

Supported Widgets

  • Reference in Production
  • Shift KPI: Target, Real Production, Delta
  • Current Hour KPI: Target, Real Production, Delta
  • Non-Quality KPI: Scrap, Rework
  • Downtime Info: Stoppage, Unclassified Duration

The start of the time frame would the orginal picking time of the rescheduled WK.

titre: [eDashBoard] Shift tracking V1 - Hours
description:
As operator, I want to see all the hour that are composing my shift. Then going on eDashBoard I have a table where each column is representing an hour of the shift. Note that starting and ending hour can start on a note rounded hour. 

For example a shift can start a 09:18 or finish at 17:39. It's not always 09:00 and 17:00

description:
As operator, I want to know if I'm in delay or in advance regarding my production and my theoretical target. Then for each hour and the current I have  delta value performed by doignt production - target, permitting to know If i'm in advance or running out of time in term of production, as screen must be consulted to far away the value must be easily read (tall font), within - in front of it, if and to highlight the delay delta will be red when negative else green.

titre: [eDashBoard] Shift tracking V1 - Hourly Target
description:
As operator, I want to know how much part shall I've been produced for the current or the past hour. the target is theoretical value calculated based on the master data. Then for each hour, I see how much part I shall have been produced. 

Note that target can have several source (depending resource type and target configuration)
Several different references can be produced during the hour/shift
For example : on the hour I produced 
REF A 20 PARTS
REF B 30 PARTS
THEN I DISPLAY 50 parts on hourly target

titre: [eDashBoard] Shift tracking V1 - Hourly Production

As operator, I want to know how many parts do I have produced on the past and current hour. Then I have for each hour of the shift a sum of the parts that has been produced

Note several different references can be produced during the hour/shift
For example : on the hour I produced 
REF A 10 PARTS
REF B 20 PARTS
THEN I DISPLAY 30 parts on hourly production

Then a vertical grid is display for the shift, the grid is without split, it's continue, it is composed of slot representing each one 5minutes, the slot can have different color, a color code is defined according tot FES

by defaut the color is "prod" green, then if a downtime ticket has openned during the hour the slot is colored according to the ticket reason. Note that there is a notion of priority in coloring stoppage are over priorized on prodution so even if we had 10 sec of stoppages (any of it) and 590 seconds of prouction for the slot of 5minutes. The slot will be colored within the stopppages classificaiton. If several stoppages are sharing the same slot, the one with the highest duration is coloring the slot.

No title are required for this column

titre: [Analyses] Implement aggregator service
description:
Given your current setup, you're looking for the best architectural approach to handle concurrent event processing and state management. The three options you've outlined represent a progression from a tactical fix to a more strategic, long-term solution.

The best approach is to add an aggregator microservice to move the lock logic and race condition handling, and just return one complete event. This is the Aggregator Pattern, and it is the recommended path for building a robust and scalable event-driven system. It provides the most significant long-term benefits despite the initial setup cost.

 

These are the options we checked at the analyses


1. Keep the Ingestion Microservice and Add a Distributed Lock

 

This is the most direct and least invasive option. You are already doing this, but it's important to formalize its pros and cons.

  • Pros:
    • Minimal Change: Requires the least amount of change to your existing architecture. You are just formalizing the logic you already have in place.
    • Direct Fix: Directly addresses the race condition in the ingestion service.
  • Cons:
    • High Complexity: The ingestion microservice now has two core responsibilities: data ingestion and complex distributed state management. This violates the Single Responsibility Principle.
    • Difficult to Scale and Maintain: Debugging becomes a major challenge. If an issue occurs, you have to trace it through the consumption logic, the distributed lock, and the state-management logic, all within the same service.
    • Tight Coupling: Your ingestion service is tightly coupled to the specifics of your event sources and the distributed locking mechanism. This makes it harder to change or extend in the future.

 

2. Add an Aggregator Microservice to Encapsulate Lock Logic and Return One Event (Recommended) 💡

 

This is the aggregator pattern. It's the most strategic choice for a long-term, scalable solution.

  • Pros:
    • Single Responsibility Principle: The aggregator microservice is a specialized service whose sole purpose is to manage state and handle concurrency for your orders. The ingestion service becomes simple and stateless, only dealing with complete events.
    • Clear and Clean Architecture: It creates a logical pipeline: 1) Events arrive, 2) The aggregator combines them into a single, complete event, and 3) The ingestion service writes the clean, complete data. This clarity is a huge benefit for maintainability and onboarding new developers.
    • Improved Scalability: You can scale each service independently. If your order creation rate is high but your picking and production updates are low, you can scale the aggregator accordingly without affecting the ingestion service.
    • Enhanced Resilience: By using a shared state store (like Redis or Cosmos DB) and implementing a distributed lock, you isolate the complexity. If an aggregator instance fails, another can pick up the partial event and continue the work. The rest of the system remains unaffected.
    • Simpler Final Ingestion: The final ingestion service doesn't need to deal with distributed locks, retries, or out-of-order events. This simplifies its code base and improves its performance.
  • Cons:
    • Increased Infrastructure: Requires a new microservice and a shared state store. This adds to your operational overhead.
    • Initial Complexity: The initial setup requires more design and implementation work to get right, including handling timeouts and partial aggregations.

 

3. Add an Aggregator to Just Forward Events to One Topic with a Common Partition Key

 

This option attempts to gain some of the benefits of the aggregator without implementing the full pattern.

  • Pros:
    • Direct Solution for Partitioning: Correctly solves the issue of related events going to different ACA instances by forcing them to the same partition.
    • Simpler Than Option 2: The aggregator service itself is just a simple router.
  • Cons:
    • Doesn't Solve the Core Problem: This approach just moves the state-management and out-of-order event problem to the ingestion service. Your ingestion service still has to manage a shared cache, handle timeouts, and wait for all three events to arrive. It's essentially performing the aggregation logic, but in a less-ideal environment.
    • No Separation of Concerns: Your ingestion service remains a complex, multi-purpose component, which is a major anti-pattern in microservices.

 

Conclusion

 

While Option 1 is the quickest fix and Option 3 offers a partial improvement, Option 2 (the aggregator pattern) is the best practice for your scenario. It's a fundamental architectural shift that isolates and solves the root cause of your concurrency issues, leading to a system that is more robust, scalable, and maintainable in the long run.

  1. Cron Expression Handling

[Design]: Ability to see non-productive times
description:
User Story Objective
The purpose of this user story is to display planned stoppages on the leveling board. This will allow users to analyze whether gaps with no WKs are due to a planned stoppage or not.

Behavior

  • Planned stoppages will be displayed only when grouping by source, regardless of the selected combination.



  • Data must be retrieved from the table [dbo].[down_time_ticket] in the production domain, where:

    • cause = 2

    • status = ACTI

  • Results should be grouped by workcenter (based on WK workcenters).

    • Database Adjustments

    • In the table down_time_ticket, add a new column: WORKCENTER.

    • Ensure ingestion from MII includes this field from [MES_FAURECIA].[dbo].[NON_TRS_TICKET].

    • Extract the following values:

      • workcenters

      • start_date

      • end_date

    Ticket Overlaps

    • If two tickets overlap in the same workcenter (e.g., the start date of one equals the end date of another), they should be merged into a single ticket with the earliest start date and the latest end date.

    Display Rules

    • Non-productive time must be represented as striped in grey.


    • The grey color code must be the same as in the downtime screen.


    • A toggle button must be added so the user can show/hide planned stoppages.

      • The button will be active by default.

[Dev][eDashBoard] Dynamic data manage by tool- Data ingestion
description:
1. Ingestion & Mapping Architecture

  • Reset & Rebuild: Reworked the ingestion layer from “single destination per source” to a fan‑out model where one source record can produce multiple destination payloads (e.g. SHIFT_TRACKING → shiftTracking + shiftTrackingDetails).
  • Mapping Flattening: MappingUtilsService.loadMappings now flattens the JSON schema so the MappingService can:
    • Resolve all destinations for a source quickly (getDestinationsForSource).
    • Map one source row into multiple structured outputs (mapAllData).
  • Timestamp & Hour Handling: Utilities enhanced (optional chaining, safer timezone lookup, local hour → UTC conversion, hex cleaning) to reduce runtime fragility.

2. Queue & Fan‑Out Processing

  • Queue Append Flow: appendAndSaveToCacheQueue updated to:
    • Derive destination list up front.
    • Map once per destination, enqueue each independently.
    • Apply plant consistency validation per mapped object.
  • Dapr Orchestration: DaprService.handleMessage refactored to:
    • Use destination-aware queues.
    • Safely guard against missing sourceTable / invalid payload.
    • Maintain per-destination processing isolation via mutex set.

3. Shift Tracking Header Logic

  • Composite Upsert: Introduced upsertByComposite using natural key (plant, resourceId, dateHourFrom) instead of relying solely on generated IDs.
    • Supports three event types (create/update/read snapshot) with overwriteAll flag.
    • Selective field assignment helper assignIf prevents accidental null overwrites unless snapshot mode.
  • 4. Shift Tracking Details Logic
  • Placeholder Strategy: Ensures a single status-only row (materialId null) can later be “converted” when first material data arrives—prevents duplicate (status + material) rows.
  • Merge Semantics:
    • Status/speed events propagate to existing material rows (or create a placeholder if none).
    • Material-specific upserts reuse placeholder row when appropriate, copying status/speed.
  • Helper Extraction: Split into applyStatusSpeed and getOrCreateMaterialRow to reduce complexity and centralize row acquisition/updates.
  • Selective Assignment: Only provided fields updated unless snapshot event (overwriteAll = true).

5. Validation & Diagnostics

  • Plant Consistency: Hardened logic (safe serialization, tolerant of missing plant in some flows, avoids noisy logs).
  • Logging Improvements:
    • Consistent contextual JobsLogContext usage.
    • Verbose vs error separation; reduced raw object dumping; safe JSON stringification for traceability.
  • Error Guards: Defensive checks in queues and Dapr message handling to avoid processing malformed or partial records.

6. Mapping JSON Enhancements

  • Multi-Destination Entries: Added destinations for both shiftTracking and shiftTrackingDetails under the same sources.
  • Detail Columns: Included new mapping for SD → slowdown in details (and header slowdown now persisted when present in payload events).
  • Flexible Key Typing: Keys define timestamp types explicitly for conversion logic.

description:

In the rework_list table under the QUA domain, calculate the total sum of the quantity column for entries that:

  • Resource_id: EB_TURBO

Rework declarations for this resource during the shift on the resource_id: EB_TURBO

  • At 2025-10-01 10:00:00 with quantity 1
  • At 2025-10-01 12:14:00 with quantity 3
  • At 2025-10-01 13:30:00 with quantity 6

Result:
Display the total scrap quantity as 1 + 3 + 6 = 10

[Design] API create order
description:
As the Dynamic Sequencer, I want to use the API CREATE ORDER to integrate orders into MES X.0 for future execution, so that production orders can be created and managed systematically.

Business Context

  • Dynamic Sequencer needs to push orders into MES X.0 for execution.

  • An API (CREATE ORDER) is required to standardize the integration process.

  • This ensures consistent, automated, and traceable order creation.

  • 1-Dynamic Sequencer has connectivity and authentication to call MES X.0 API.

  • 2-API must follow MES X.0 standards for authentication and error handling.

  • 3-Database changes to store new order attributes if not already present.

  • API: CREATE ORDER – Required Fields

    1. Plant Id

    2. Order Id (PIK code)

    3. Material Number

    4. Ordered Quantity

    5. Grouping Key

    6. Work Center (WC)

    7. Resource

    8. Sequence Number

    9. Is Frozen (values: 1 = Yes, 0 = No)

    10. Linked WK

    • All fields marked as mandatory must be validated.

    • Is Frozen must be a Boolean indicator (0 or 1).

    • Order Id must be unique per Plant.

    Target Table Structure

    Table name: MES_PRODUCTION_ORDER

    Column Name               Data Type                     NullableDescription
    PLANT_ID VARCHAR(4) NOT NULL Plant identifier
    ORDER_ID VARCHAR() NOT NULL Production Order ID (unique)
    MATERIAL_NUMBER VARCHAR(18) NOT NULL Material reference
    ORDERED_QTY INT NOT NULL Quantity ordered
    QUANTITY_DONE INT NOT NULL Quantity already produced (default = 0)
    STATUS VARCHAR(15) NULL Order status 
    GROUPING_KEY VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL Grouping information
    WORKCENTER VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL Work Center code
    RESOURCE VARCHAR(20) NULL Resource assigned
    SEQUENCE_NUMBER INT NOT NULL Order sequence number
    IS_FROZEN BIT NOT NULL 1 = frozen, 0 = not frozen
    LINKED_WK VARCHAR() NULL Linked Work Order/Key

    • Quantity Done + Status are managed internally by MES, not API input

    Functional Checks

    1. Mandatory Fields Validation

      • PLANT_ID, ORDER_ID, MATERIAL_NUMBER, ORDERED_QTY, WORKCENTER, Sequence Number, Grouping Key,IS_FROZEN must be provided.

    2. Uniqueness

      • ORDER_ID must be unique within the same PLANT_ID.

    3. Data Rules

      • ORDERED_QTY > 0

      • QUANTITY_DONE ≤ ORDERED_QTY

      • IS_FROZEN ∈ {0,1}

    4. Referential Checks

      • WORKCENTER must exist in the Work Center HRY table.

      • check if material is produced under that Workcenter or not (check for production version)

      • RESOURCE must be valid if provided and match with the Workcenter 

      • Material number must

    5. Default Behavior

      • QUANTITY_DONE initialized to 0.

      • CREATED_AT set automatically by the system.

    6. Error Handling

      • If validation fails → return HTTP 400 with specific error message.

    Workcenter doesn't exist 
    Material doesn't exist
    order already exist
    Resource is not linked to Workcenter
    Quantity must be integer

description:
As the Dynamic Sequencer, I want to use the API UPDATE ORDER to modify existing production orders in MES X.0, so that order details can be adapted based on real production needs.

Business Context

  • After an order is created in MES X.0, Dynamic Sequencer may need to update certain fields (quantity, grouping, sequencing, etc.).

  • This ensures MES reflects real-time planning decisions and supports flexibility.

  • Some updates (e.g., resource changes).

  • Business alignment is still needed to finalize update rules and restrictions.

Dynamic Sequencer can update only:

  • Ordered Quantity

  • Grouping Key

  • Work Center (WC)

  • Resource (optional)

  • Sequence Number

  • Is Frozen

  • Linked WK

Mandatory Checks

  • PLANT_ID, ORDER_ID, MATERIAL_NUMBER must be provided (not updatable).

  • The order must exist before update.

Updatable Field Rules

  • ORDERED_QTY > 0 and ≥ QUANTITY_DONE.

  • GROUPING_KEY can be modified but must respect allowed business rules.

  • WORKCENTER must exist in the Work Center master.

  • RESOURCE optional, must be valid if provided.

  • SEQUENCE_NUMBER can only be updated if IS_FROZEN = 0.

  • IS_FROZEN ∈ {0,1}.

  • LINKED_WK valid only in FG cases.

Perform a detailed analysis of how Azure Application Insights can be effectively integrated into the application layer to enhance observability and traceability across environments (dev, pre-prod, prod).

  • Architecture proposal including telemetry pipeline flow and data collection model.

  • List of required configuration or dependency changes in both application and infrastructure repositories.

Expected Outcome:
A validated understanding of how to integrate and scale Azure Application Insights across our NestJS microservices while maintaining compliance with performance and security standards.

[DEV Task] Analysis Task
description:
🧩 Issue Summary

During the go-live of GOW for EWM, the team observed unexpected behavior:
a large number of transfer events were triggered — including for materials not flagged as EWM.

🔍 Root Cause Analysis

After investigation, the issue was traced to the SQL query used in the endpoint
material/GetEwmMaterialList.

In the original query: 

SELECT  
    mDtl.plant AS plant,
    (
        SELECT 
            material_dtl.material_id AS material
        FROM 
            material_dtl 
        WHERE 
            material_dtl.plant = mDtl.plant
        FOR JSON PATH
    ) AS materials
FROM 
    material_dtl AS mDtl
INNER JOIN 
    material 
    ON material.material_id = mDtl.material_id
WHERE 
    material.ewm_flow = 1
    AND mDtl.plant IN (1665)
GROUP BY 
    mDtl.plant;

the condition: 

WHERE material.ewm_flow = 1

was applied only in the outer query, not inside the JSON subquery.

❗What Happens in Practice

  1. The outer query filters records in mDtl and material for rows where ewm_flow = 1.

  2. However, the subquery: 

    SELECT material_dtl.material_id FROM material_dtl WHERE material_dtl.plant = mDtl.plant

    runs without any EWM filtering.

  3. As a result, the JSON array includes all materials for the plant, not just those flagged as EWM.

This means that even if only some materials are EWM-enabled, the query still returns every material, leading to incorrect downstream transfers.

So if a plant has 100 materials but only 5 are EWM (`ewm_flow = 1`), the query will still produce a JSON array containing all 100 — because the `FOR JSON PATH` subquery doesn’t know about `ewm_flow`.

✅ Correct Query

To ensure that only EWM materials are fetched, the filtering condition must be applied inside the JSON subquery: 

SELECT  
    mDtl.plant AS plant,
    (
        SELECT 
            md.material_id AS material
        FROM 
            material_dtl AS md
        INNER JOIN 
            material AS m
            ON m.material_id = md.material_id
        WHERE 
            md.plant = mDtl.plant
            AND m.ewm_flow = 1
        FOR JSON PATH
    ) AS materials
FROM 
    material_dtl AS mDtl
WHERE 
    mDtl.plant IN (1665)
GROUP BY 
    mDtl.plant;

This ensures:

  • The subquery joins material explicitly,

  • Applies the m.ewm_flow = 1 filter within the JSON context,

  • And returns only EWM materials per plant.

🧪 Validation Step

To confirm this hypothesis, we performed a controlled test:
we selected a material not flagged as EWM and executed a transfer for it.

Unexpectedly, the event was still generated — confirming that the original query included non-EWM materials in its result set, as illustrated below:


ts is 1760000210: Thursday, October 9, 2025 9:56:50 AM (time of trf)


This behavior clearly validates that the issue originates from the query logic.

🧾 Summary

Result

Outer query only (location of is_ewm=1)

Filters which plants are shown, but the JSON array still contains all materials

Inside JSON subquery

Filters the JSON array to include only EWM materials ✅

Both

Redundant but safe — ensures consistent filtering across all levels

description:
After moving to production, it was observed that events in the Event Hub queue were added but not consumed, resulting in a backlog. When the ingestion service was deployed, it started processing historical events, causing delays.

Investigation findings:

  • The backlog accumulated due to unconsumed events prior to deployment.

  • Processing of historical events caused significant delays of data ingestion in prod

To restore normal processing and skip historical events, the offset in the checkpoint blobs will need to be advanced to start consuming only the latest incoming data.

[Design]: Live status x resources
description:
Business Context

Today, the Gap Leader is responsible for multiple machines (resources) but does not have a global view of the data linked to each one.
To understand the situation, the Gap Leader needs to navigate through several dashboards or systems, which is time-consuming and makes it difficult to react quickly to deviations.

The Live Status View will centralize the most important data in one screen, allowing the Gap Leader to:

  • See the status of routines running in the Gap.

  • Monitor key KPIs per resource (Target, Produced, Delta, Scrap).

  • Identify issues or delays instantly.

  • Access each resource’s detailed eDashboard in one click.

This feature enhances real-time decision-making, visibility, and reactivity on the shop floor.

Additionally, the list of available Gaps will not be static but automatically extracted from an external tool mLean.

Functional Scope

The new screen will allow:

  1. Gap Selection

    • The user selects a Gap from a dropdown list .

  2. Resource Display

    • Once a Gap is selected, all resources (machines) belonging to that Gap are displayed.

  3. KPI Display by resource

    • Each resource card shows the following KPIs for the current shift:

      • Resource description

      • Target

      • Produced

      • Delta

      • Scrap

  4. KPI Display in The live status header:
  • First OK part
  • Routines
  • TPM
  • Managment Control
  • Shift Delta
  • Alert Status

     5.Navigation

    • By clicking on a resource, the user is redirected to that resource’s eDashboard for detailed analysis.

    • the user can have a quick acces to the GAP by just putting the name in the URL (same as edashboard)


Scenario Multiple Resources

  • The user enters the Live Status screen.

  • The system identifies the Gap Leader’s scope and loads:

    • The list of resources with live KPIs.


HIERARCHY : 

The filter (dropdown list) shows a list of gaps and their resources.

When clicking on the GAP, the user is redirected to the live status 1:n 

When clicking on the resource, we have 2 cases: 

  1. If there are multiple resources assigned to the GAP > the user is redirected to the live status 1:n 
  2. If only 1 resource is assigned to the gap > the user is redirected to the live status 1:1

Interaction behaviors :

  • Live status > edashboard : 

From the screen live status 1:n > the user is able to go to the edashboard by clicking on the resource 

  • Interaction behavior edashboard > live status :

From the edashboard > the user is able to go back to the live status 1:n filtered by the GAP and team info

titre: [Design] Shift delta
description:

    • Displayed at the top of the dashboard as general information.

    • Calculated as the sum of deltas from all resources in the mLean Gap.

titre: [Design] mLean widget
description:
• The TPM status widget provides visibility on the number of Total Productive Maintenance (TPM) actions to perform during the selected shift for the current gap.

  • It calculates the ratio of successfully performed TPM actions (TpmOk / Total TPM items) based on data retrieved for the given ShiftStart and ShiftEnd time window and the gap perimeter taken from mLean via external API.

  • The widget is automatically refreshed every minute, ensuring near real-time visibility for the Gap Leader.

  • For each TPM item, the result value is evaluated:

    • 0 → NOK (not OK)

    • -2 → Not Assessed

    • Any other value → OK

    TpmOk is calculated as the count of items where result ≠ -2

  • The widget’s background color reflects the defined logic:

    • If there is any NOK (0) → background RED.

    • For the current shift, if no NOK but at least one Not Assessed (−2) → background YELLOW.

    If all items are OK → background GREEN.
  • In case of data retrieval issues, the widget shows “Data unavailable” in neutral background (gray).

titre: {Design]mLean widget routinr
description:
• The routine status widget retrieves data from the external mLean system via an exposed API.

  • The mLean system provides an API  exposing routine data with their ID and status.

  • The widget displays:

    • The total number of routines (Y) assigned for the selected shift.

    • The number of routines completed  (X).

    • The calculated ratio X/Y.

  • The background color of the widget changes dynamically based on completion status and shift timing.

  • MES X.0 will:

    1. Call the mLean API at regular intervals to fetch the list of routines for the current or selected shift.

    2. extract the status for each routine.

    3. Apply business logic to calculate:

      • Done: status = OK or N/A

      • Not done: any other status

    4. Compute ratio: X = count of “Done”, Y = total number of routines.

    5. Display X/Y and apply background color according to the logic below.

  • X = Y → background color is green.

  • X < Y → background color is yellow.

titre: [Design]: X resources KPI widget
description:
• The view displays a summary of key performance indicators (KPIs) for each resource managed by the Gap Leader.

  • For every resource under the gap perimeter, the following KPIs are shown (same rules in e-dashboard):

    • Target (planned production quantity)

    • Prod (actual production quantity)

    • Delta (difference between Target and Prod)

    • Scrap (quantity of nonconforming parts)

  • The KPIs are displayed in a tabular, providing a quick and clear overview of each resource’s performance.

  • The data should be retrieved in real-time (or refreshed based on the defined refresh interval of the dashboard).

    • For the order of display of resources at this step we'll go alphabetically based on resource description.

titre: {Design] Management control
description:
KPI Formula:

The KPI displays a fraction representing ControlAssessed / Number of Items​

  • ControlAssessed: Calculated based on the item status, considering only statuses 1, 0, and -2.

  • Number of Items: Includes all statuses — 1, 0, -2, and NULL.


Dynamic Background Color Logic
The KPI background color changes dynamically according to the following conditions:
  • General Rule (except for the first hour of a shift):

    • 🟥 RED:

      • There is at least one NOK (Not OK) item in the current hour, or

      • There was at least one NOK item in the previous hour.

    • 🟧 ORANGE:

      • There is at least one Not Assessed item in the previous hour.

    • 🟨 YELLOW:

      • There is at least one Not Assessed item in the current hour.

    • 🟩 GREEN:

      • Only OK and N/A items remain (no NOK and no Not Assessed).


  • Special Case — First Hour of the Shift:

    Since only the current shift is relevant, the previous hour is not considered.

    • 🟥 RED: If there is at least one NOK item in the current hour.

    • 🟨 YELLOW: If there is at least one Not Assessed item in the current hour.

    • 🟩 GREEN: If all items are OK (no NOK, no Not Assessed).


    • Additional Notes

    • The KPI automatically refreshes every minute.

    • The KPI title can be translated according to the user’s language preference.

    • The number of statuses (items) is identical for all hours.

    • The KPI values should reset on an hourly basis to reflect only the data from the current hour or current hour and previous hour only.

    • The check on previous hour considers only H-1.

    • The label represents the hour of the shift. For example, during the first hour, we retrieve the statuses associated with label 1 for the various IDs we have. The labels then increment by one for each hour.

      In other words, label 1 always corresponds to the first hour of the current shift, label 2 to the second hour, and so on.

description:
Following the highlighted issue related to incorrect target and production data display for a resource managed by part in the eDashboard (PPR), it was observed that when production switches from Part A to Part B, the target, production, and list of references in production are displayed incorrectly.

After investigation and detailed analysis, the root cause was identified as a discrepancy in the slowdown values between the two materials. In the API, we are currently grouping data by the slowdown field, which leads to inconsistencies when different materials have different slowdown values.



After further verification with @LANDOULSI Baraa, it was confirmed that the issue originates from ingesting the wrong column — the system currently uses the SD column from the SHIFT_TRACKING table instead of the correct SLOWDOWN column. The SLOWDOWN value should be used because it remains consistent for the same hour regardless of the reference, whereas the SD column serves a different purpose.

Proposed Solution:
Update the data ingestion logic to use the correct source column (SLOWDOWN) for the MES slowdown field in the resource-di mapping.

titre: add tokenRefreshIntervalSeconds
[ANALYSIS]/ [eDashboard] No data is displayed in the Shift Tracking section or in the KPI widgets on the eDashboard
description:
Following the identified issue where data was not displayed on the eDashboard in PPR, my investigation revealed that the problem is caused by several contributing factors detailed below:

1. Redis Client Error


The Redis Client Error: read ECONNRESET means that the TCP connection between our Node.js application and the Redis server was forcibly closed by the remote host (Redis).
This is not a bug in our code but indicates that the connection was unexpectedly dropped at the network or Redis level.

 Several errors in the logs confirm this:

[31m[Nest] 18 - [39m10/22/2025, 11:56:41 PM [31m ERROR[39m [38;5;3m[JobsLoggerService] [39m[31m{"context":{"method":"createConnection","service":"RedisConnectionFactory","userId":"MESXSystem"},"message":"Redis Client Error:","timestamp":"2025-10-22T23:56:41.401Z","error":"read ECONNRESET","stack":"Error: read ECONNRESET\n at TLSWrap.onStreamRead (node/stream_base_commons:216:20)"}[39m]

Following that, multiple logs show reauthentication attempts triggered by these errors:

[33m[Nest] 18 - [39m10/22/2025, 11:56:41 PM [33m WARN[39m [38;5;3m[JobsLoggerService] [39m[33m{"context":{"method":"createConnection","service":"RedisConnectionFactory","userId":"MESXSystem"},"message":"Reauthenticating due to auth error or connection reset","timestamp":"2025-10-22T23:56:41.401Z"}[39m

2. Redis Heartbeat Mechanism


The logs also show the Redis heartbeat behavior:

[32m[Nest] 19 - [39m10/22/2025, 11:57:03 PM [32m LOG[39m [38;5;3m[JobsLoggerService] [39m[32m{"context":{"method":"startHeartbeat","service":"RedisConnectionFactory","userId":"MESXSystem"},"message":"Starting Redis heartbeat","timestamp":"2025-10-22T23:57:03.545Z"}[39m

However, there is also an error indicating a failed heartbeat ping:

[32m[Nest] 18 - [39m10/22/2025, 11:56:41 PM [32m LOG[39m [38;5;3m[JobsLoggerService] [39m[32m{"context":{"method":"startHeartbeat","service":"RedisConnectionFactory","userId":"MESXSystem"},"message":"Redis heartbeat ping failed","timestamp":"2025-10-22T23:56:41.403Z"}[39m

In the code, when the ping fails, the system triggers a refreshTokenWithRetry (in our case, using an access key).
The reauthentication process also failed, as shown by the following errors:

[31m[Nest] 18 - [39m10/22/2025, 11:56:46 PM [31m ERROR[39m [38;5;3m[JobsLoggerService] [39m[31m{"context":{"method":"handleReconnection","service":"RedisConnectionFactory","userId":"MESXSystem"},"message":"Failed to reconnect Redis clients: TimeoutError: ResourceRequest timed out","timestamp":"2025-10-22T23:56:46.820Z"}[39m

[31m[Nest] 18 - [39m10/22/2025, 11:56:46 PM [31m ERROR[39m [38;5;3m[JobsLoggerService] [39m[31m{"context":{"method":"refreshRedisTokenWithRetry","service":"RedisConnectionFactory","userId":"MESXSystem"},"message":"Error refreshing Redis token: TimeoutError: ResourceRequest timed out","timestamp":"2025-10-22T23:56:46.820Z"}[39m

3. Pool Draining Error


I also found errors today related to the connection pool being drained:

[31m[Nest] 18 - [39m10/23/2025, 9:59:42 AM [31m ERROR[39m [38;5;3m[JobsLoggerService] [39m[31m{"context":{"method":"validateAndTrackChanges","service":"validation","userId":"MESXSystem"},"message":"Error while verifying and tracking ingestion event for table "SHIFT_TRACKING": pool is draining and cannot accept work","timestamp":"2025-10-23T09:59:42.669Z"}[39m

 {"context":{"method":"getClient","service":"RedisConnectionFactory","userId":"MESXSystem"},"message":"Error acquiring Redis client from pool","timestamp":"2025-10-23T09:59:42.665Z","error":"pool is draining and cannot accept work"

(“Pool is draining” means that the connection pool is in the process of closing and cannot handle new requests — typically triggered when Redis or the database client begins shutting down or encounters repeated connection failures.)

4. JavaScript Heap Out of Memory

Another critical error observed:

FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory

This indicates that the Node.js process ran out of memory, likely due to unhandled retries or accumulated pending operations caused by the Redis connection instability.

5. Input Binding (Shift Tracking) Errors

Several errors were also found related to input bindings for shift tracking:

time="2025-10-23T03:21:06.741439672Z" level=warning msg="Error processing EventHubs events for topic dbz.cpt.cpt_faurecia.dbo.shift_tracking. Error: %!v(MISSING). Retrying..." app_id=rsrce-di component="bindings-cpt-faurecia-dbo-shift-tracking-rsrce-di (bindings.azure.eventhubs/v1)" instance=ca-gptmpxp01-eun-ppr-rsrce-di--0000003-8bcf4994b-46rw4 scope=dapr.contrib type=log ver=1.13.6-msft.

This occurred because the pool was already saturated and could not process additional events.

In addition, we’ve been receiving multiple alerts related to the DTU usage of the RSRCE database in the PPR environment.

From my analysis, I believe we should reconsider the eDashboard design.
It would be more reliable to implement it as a materialized view, where data insertions occur at the Cosmos DB level, ensuring better performance and reducing data loss.

As a workaround, I performed a manual restart of the container and continued to monitor the system’s behavior.
I also created snapshots to correct the data, and it is now accurate in the database. 



For the second shift, the data is displayed correctly.

Proposed Solution:

  • Increase Connection Pool Capacity (increase REDIS_POOL_MAX_CONNECTIONS)
  • Enhance the Redis reconnection mechanism to handle heartbeat failures, preventing unnecessary token refresh when using an access key.

description:
Technical Report: Analysis of High DTU Usage for RSRCE in PPR

1️⃣ Executive Summary

The RSRCE domain is experiencing high DTU usage (>90%) in Azure SQL. Azure flagged a high-consuming query related to shift_tracking_details and recommended creating a non-clustered index on (shift_tracking_id, material_id). However, no explicit query in the codebase filters or joins on these two fields.




After a detailed analysis, the root cause is traced to TypeORM generating hidden queries to resolve ManyToOne relationships. This report explains the issue, provides evidence, and outlines optimization strategies.

2️⃣ Context and Problem Statement

  • Endpoint: getHourlyAggregatedProduction

  • Purpose: Aggregate production data per hour for a given plant, resource, and shift.

  • Observed Issue: Azure SQL Portal flagged a high-consuming query: 

(@0 int,@1 nvarchar(11))
SELECT DISTINCT "distinctAlias"."ShiftTrackingDetails_shift_tracking_details_id" AS "ids_ShiftTrackingDetails_shift_tracking_details_id"
FROM (
    SELECT ...
    FROM "shift_tracking_details" "ShiftTrackingDetails"
    LEFT JOIN "shift_tracking" "ShiftTrackingDetails__ShiftTrackingDetails_shiftTracking"
        ON "ShiftTrackingDetails__ShiftTrackingDetails_shiftTracking"."shift_tracking_id" = "ShiftTrackingDetails"."shift_tracking_id"
        AND ("ShiftTrackingDetails__ShiftTrackingDetails_shiftTracking"."deleted_at" IS NULL)
    WHERE 
        "ShiftTrackingDetails__ShiftTrackingDetails_shiftTracking"."shift_tracking_id" = @0
        AND "ShiftTrackingDetails"."material_id" = @1
        AND "ShiftTrackingDetails"."deleted_at" IS NULL
) "distinctAlias"
ORDER BY "ShiftTrackingDetails_shift_tracking_details_id" ASC
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY

  • Observation: This query is not written explicitly in the codebase.

3️⃣ Entity Relationship Overview

ShiftTracking (Parent) 

@Entity('shift_tracking')
export class ShiftTracking extends TimeStamp {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() shiftTrackingId: number;
  @Column() plant: number;
  @Column() resourceId: string;
  @Column() dateHourFrom: Date;
  ...
}

ShiftTrackingDetails (Child) 

@Entity('shift_tracking_details')
export class ShiftTrackingDetails extends TimeStamp {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() shiftTrackingDetailsId: number;

  @ManyToOne(() => ShiftTracking, { onDelete: 'CASCADE' })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'shift_tracking_id' })
  shiftTracking: ShiftTracking;

  @Column() materialId: string;
  @Column() toolId: string;
  ...
}

  • Relationship: ShiftTrackingDetails → ShiftTracking (ManyToOne)

  • Accessing properties from ShiftTracking in DTOs can trigger additional queries.

4️⃣ TypeORM Behavior and Hidden Query Generation

  • TypeORM generates extra SQL queries to resolve ManyToOne relations when related entity properties are accessed.

  • Example: Accessing detail.shiftTracking triggers: 

SELECT DISTINCT ...
FROM shift_tracking_details
LEFT JOIN shift_tracking ...
WHERE shift_tracking_id = @0 AND material_id = @1
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY

  • This query is internal, not explicitly written in the application.

Diagram: Query Flow 

Application Endpoint: getHourlyAggregatedProduction
       |
       v
TypeORM QueryBuilder -> Aggregation Query (raw SQL)
       |
       +--> Accessing detail.shiftTracking triggers hidden query
              |
              v
    SELECT DISTINCT ... FROM shift_tracking_details LEFT JOIN shift_tracking ...

5️⃣ Original Endpoint Query 

const rows = await this.shiftTrackingRepository
  .createQueryBuilder('st')
  .innerJoin('shift_tracking_details', 'd', 'd.shiftTracking = st.shiftTrackingId')
  .where('st.plant = :plant', { plant })
  .andWhere('st.resourceId = :resourceId', { resourceId })
  .andWhere('st.dateShiftStart = :shiftStartDate', { shiftStartDate })
  .andWhere('st.dateShiftEnd = :shiftEndDate', { shiftEndDate })
  .select([
    "RIGHT('0' + CAST(DATEPART(HOUR, st.dateHourFrom) AS VARCHAR(2)), 2) AS hour",
    'st.dateHourFrom AS dateHourFrom',
    'st.dateHourTo AS dateHourTo',
    'd.status AS status',
    'd.speed AS speed',
    'd.slowdown AS slowdown',
    'd.toolId AS toolId',
    'SUM(d.targetQty) AS target',
    'SUM(d.realQty) AS production',
    "STRING_AGG(d.materialId, ';') AS material",
  ])
  .groupBy('st.dateHourFrom')
  .addGroupBy('st.dateHourTo')
  .addGroupBy('d.status')
  .addGroupBy('d.speed')
  .addGroupBy('d.slowdown')
  .addGroupBy('d.toolId')
  .orderBy('st.dateHourFrom', 'ASC')
  .getRawMany();

  • Aggregates hourly production without triggering additional hidden queries if relation fields are not accessed in DTO mapping.

6️⃣ Recommendation and Optimization

  1. Implement the Azure-recommended index to improve performance: 

CREATE INDEX IX_shift_tracking_details_shift_tracking_material
ON shift_tracking_details(shift_tracking_id, material_id)
  1. Monitor DTU usage after applying the index and adjusting the code.

7️⃣ Conclusion

  • Root Cause: Hidden TypeORM query due to ManyToOne relation resolution.

  • Impact: High DTU usage and flagged queries in Azure.

  • Solution: Implement the suggested index.

Index Optimization Recommendation

Azure Portal also recommends removing the duplicate index IDX_SHIFT_TRACKING_COMPOSITE.


Analysis:

  • The entity has both: 

 
 
 
@Unique('UQ_SHIFT_TRACKING', ['plant', 'resourceId', 'dateHourFrom'])
@Index('IDX_SHIFT_TRACKING_COMPOSITE', ['plant', 'resourceId', 'dateHourFrom'])

  • In SQL Server, a unique constraint automatically creates a non-clustered index on the specified columns.

  • The IDX_SHIFT_TRACKING_COMPOSITE index is therefore redundant, creating two indexes on the same columns, which wastes storage and adds unnecessary maintenance overhead.

  • Removing the duplicate index will simplify the indexing structure without impacting performance, as the unique constraint already provides the necessary index for query optimization.

Solution:

  • Remove the duplicate index IDX_SHIFT_TRACKING_COMPOSITE.

  • Keep the unique constraint UQ_SHIFT_TRACKING to enforce data integrity and indexing.

Summary:

  • ✅ Keep: UQ_SHIFT_TRACKING (provides uniqueness + index)

  • ✅ Remove: IDX_SHIFT_TRACKING_COMPOSITE (duplicate)

  • ✅ Add: Azure-recommended index on (shift_tracking_id, material_id)

This approach optimizes performance, reduces unnecessary overhead, and aligns with best practices.
